title: The systems
text:
I build Situ as small systems, made to inform the design of a game (research-creation). Each has one job, a blueprint and its own tests, and I try it in the Lab before the next one may use it. The status word says how far each one stands (what the words mean).
Each system has an overview page, which says what it found, and a page on how it is built and tested. The job each one does in a game is on From systems to a game. To follow one number from its source to the Lab, see Tracing a result.

title: The systems
text:
Reading the diagrams
Every blueprint uses the same key. A grey outline is data coming in. A dashed grey one is a decision I made and kept in a file. A white outline is a processing step, and a thick white one is a result written to disk. Pink marks a test.
On the map sheets, labels never overlap. When a label has to move, a thin line points back to what it names.

title: Checking the sources
text:
Signs: what they mean
The Québec standard for road signs, Tome V, Signalisation routière, costs money and was out of my reach, so I used free sources. The Règlement sur la signalisation routière on LégisQuébec, current to 1 June 2026, gives the legal meaning of each kind of sign. The ministry’s 2026 posters (Québec.ca) and its online catalogue, the Répertoire des dispositifs, give their names and pictures.








Article
Sign
Meaning

The code numbers differ between sources. The regulation numbers the turn bans P-110-6 to P-110-8, while the 2026 poster shows P-110-62 for “no left turn”. So S3 reads a sign’s written meaning and ignores its code.
None of these sources says where a sign stands, before or after the junction. The only text on placement I found is a 2001 provincial guide quoting Tome V. It says turn signs stand “à proximité de l’endroit où la manœuvre doit être effectuée”, near where the turn is made (BAnQ). That does not say which corner. So placement has to be read from photos, one junction at a time.

title: Checking the sources
section: PlanX: how far is a radius?
text:
PlanX: how far is a radius?
PlanX is the QGIS tool that gives each street segment its space syntax values (what these are). Two of them are choice, roughly how often a street lies on the way between other places, and integration, roughly how easy it is to reach. Each is measured within a radius. Its manual (version 4.18, September 2026) calls the radius “metric radii in map units”. It does not say whether 800 m runs along the streets or in a straight line, and those give two very different neighbourhoods.
PlanX reports how many other segments each one found within the radius. For twelve Griffintown segments I counted again in two ways. The first count was the segments I can walk to within the radius. The second was those whose middle lies inside a circle of that radius. At 800 m, PlanX’s counts came to 0.89 of the walking counts and 0.57 of the circle counts. At 400 m they came to 0.92 and 0.53.
So the radius is measured along the streets (verified), and S2 reads it that way. PlanX’s counts sit a little under mine. Most likely it measures metres along the path with the fewest turns, which is a bit longer than the shortest (assumption). I could not reproduce the counts exactly, so that detail stays open.
The manual also says the network has no direction. So the vehicle values describe the street layout without its one-way rules. I checked PlanX’s normalised forms of choice and integration against the published papers in Reading closely. These forms, NACH and NAIN, can be compared between networks of different sizes. NACH matches Hillier, Yang and Turner (2012, p. 191) exactly. PlanX also counts each pair of segments once, the same definition as Turner (2007, p. 544) (how I found out). For NAIN the paper gives two other forms. They put the streets in the same order, and the numbers compare only within one form.

title: Checking the sources
section: Mapillary: which way does a sign face?
text:
Mapillary: which way does a sign face?
Mapillary reads its street photos by machine and maps every sign it sees, with a compass angle. If that angle is the way the sign faces, it can settle which street a sign controls.

Getting the signs
I asked Mapillary for every feature it has mapped around the S1 network. I asked in squares of about 400 m, because it refuses large ones. I kept the traffic signs unchanged, with their dates. On 10 October that gave 1,455 signs. Of these, 838 were regulatory, among them 235 stop detections and 88 no-entry signs.


Testing the direction on signs we already know
A stop sign faces the drivers it stops. For every city stop post, S3 already knows which street those drivers arrive along. So the right answer is known in advance. For each city stop post I took the nearest Mapillary stop sign within 15 m and compared.



Left: the idea. Right: the test. Pink bars are posts where Mapillary’s angle is within 45° of facing the drivers.


Of 139 city stop posts, 99 had a Mapillary stop sign within 15 m. For 69 of those, the angle was within 45° of facing the drivers. Only one pointed the way they travel. The typical (median) difference was 21°.
So the angle is the way the sign faces (partial). A smaller group sits near 90° off, and the cause is simple (partial). At an all-way stop, four stop signs stand within a few metres, and the nearest one can face the cross street. The main peak sits about 15° off zero, and I do not know why yet. Fifteen degrees never confuses two streets meeting at a junction, so it does not change how I use the angle. Still, a machine reading is evidence to check. Where a sign’s placement was in doubt, S3 uses Mapillary’s facing and then the photo itself (S3 checks with photos).

title: How S9 is built
text:
The readings
All three readings use the same S1 streets, with the same starts and ends. A route is a chain of streets joined at junctions, and a walker may not turn back along the street just walked. “Shortest” adds up metres. “Open” adds up metres weighted by how enclosed each street is: the street with the smallest area seen in S8 counts at 1.5 times its length, and the most open one at its plain length. “Straight” adds up the degrees turned at each junction, from the direction a walker arrives in to the direction of the next street. Length only breaks ties.

title: How S9 is built
text:
The comparison
S9 reads the counts and space syntax only after the flows are made. At each counted junction, it sets each reading’s commuters against the mean number of pedestrians the city counted there at 7 and 8 h. For every walkable street inside the area, it ranks the morning’s flow against walking choice and integration, and gives a rank correlation. Beyond the doors, it sets the commuters’ straight legs against the ring’s weekday counts, next to the expectations I wrote before reading the ring (outputs/s9/expected.csv). The comparison describes. It does not pick a reading.

text:

Ten checks
Each check asks one plain question of what S9 wrote. Nine must pass, and all nine do. The tenth only reports.









Question
Answer




T1
Do the walkers add up to what S7 says, kind by kind, worked out again from the S7 tables?
yes, all six kinds


T2

yes: 16,958 trips × 3 readings


T3
Is the “shortest” route really the shortest walk?
yes, against S7’s own code, on every 20th trip


T4
Does each reading win by its own rule?
yes: “straight” never turns more than another reading, and “open” never walks more than 1.5 times the shortest


T5
Are the flows on streets and junctions the sum of the routes that use them?
yes


T6
Were the flows made without the counts and space syntax?
yes: run again with both scrambled, no route moves


T7
Does the comparison with the counts follow from the flows and the S5 table?
yes: 7 junctions × 2 hours


T8

yes: 13 assumptions and 5 pieces of evidence


T9

yes, worked out again: 23 sites


T10

I added half a person to one street’s flow at 8 h, and T5 caught it. T6 first failed because it found the words “counts” and “space syntax” in the description at the top of the code. It now reads the code alone.

text:
The sources



Source
What S8 takes from it




S1 Streets
the walkable segments inside the area, and their lines


OpenStreetMap buildings, through the Overpass API, fetched 2026-10-14, ODbL
1,682 building outlines over the area and 150 m around it; 14 buildings stored as “relations” have no outline in the file, so they stop nothing

title: How S8 is built
text:
Viewpoints
Each walkable segment (a stretch of street as S1 draws it) inside the area is cut into steps of about 10 m. A viewpoint stands at the middle of each step, on the street’s centreline where the S1 line runs. A segment shorter than 10 m gets one viewpoint.

title: How S8 is built
text:
Sight lines
From each viewpoint, 360 sight lines leave, one per degree. Each stops at the first building edge it crosses, or at 300 m. A line passing exactly through a building’s corner counts as stopped there, so it cannot slip between two edges.

title: How S8 is built
text:
Measures







Measure
What it says




area
the surface inside the ends of the 360 lines, in m²


perimeter
the length of that shape’s outline


longest and mean sight line
the furthest you can see, and how far on average


compactness
4π × area / perimeter²: 1 for a circle, small for a long thin corridor


open share
the share of lines that reach 300 m


beyond share
the share of lines that end outside the box of buildings S8 read, where the view is unknown



Benedikt (1979) defined the isovist and several of these measures. Batty (2001) uses compactness to compare isovist shapes across a plan. Turner and others (2001) extend isovists into visibility graphs, which S8 does not build.

TipTesting the tests



T2 first failed on 16 viewpoints, by up to 9 m². The check started from the positions saved in the file, rounded to the centimetre. A centimetre was enough to let a line graze past a corner it had hit before. T2 now places the viewpoints again from S1. A smaller gap of 0.1 m² remained: the area was summed in coordinates of about five million metres, which loses decimals. S8 now sums it from the viewpoint outwards, and the two agree.

title: How S7 is built
text:
Commuters per home
A building with homes takes its tract’s commuters per home and its tract’s mix of ways to work. A building in a tract where nobody lived at the 2021 census would take the combined rates of the lived-in tracts and become a checkpoint, a case set aside for a closer look. None does.

title: How S7 is built
text:
The one correction
The census week fell during the pandemic. S7 reduces each tract’s share working from home by the fall measured across Canada, from 24.3 % in May 2021 to 17.4 % in May 2025. For the people who come here to work, the census does not say how many worked from home. So S7 raises their number by the national change alone, about 9 %. The hour bands keep the census’s own widths: S7 does not spread them into single hours.

title: How S7 is built
text:
The nearest stops
For every building with homes, S7 measures the walk to the nearest metro entrance and to the nearest bus stop with a weekday departure. The walk follows the walkable S1 streets, from the point where the building meets its street. A stop outside the area is reached through the S1 door (a point where a street leaves the area) that makes the walk shortest. The part beyond the door is measured as a straight line, so a distance to a stop outside is a little short.

Seven checks

Question
Answer

report









TipTesting the tests



The first version of S7 drew walkers on every street, hour by hour. To do that it had to imagine where each person goes and when they come back, so I took that part out: it belongs to S9. Run twice on the same input, S7 gives the same output (X1). X2 changes the one correction. With working from home as in May 2021, about 5,400 residents commute. With today’s national figure it is 7,200, and at the 2016 level about 9,700. The shares by mode and hour do not move.

title: How S6 is built and tested
section: Values as the source gives them
text:
Values as the source gives them
S6 copies each value and changes none. A tree with no planting date keeps an empty date and the reason, and a bench with no tags in OpenStreetMap keeps none. A hydrant whose installation date is the city’s placeholder, 1 January 1900, keeps no date.

title: How S6 is built and tested
text:
Objects found in photos
Mapillary’s software may place one object twice, or see a pole’s two heads as two lights. So S6 joins detections of one kind lying within 3 m of each other, in a chain, and places the object at their mean. Each object keeps every detection it holds, with the dates of the first and last photo that show it. Zebra stripes and plain crosswalk lines both count as a crossing.
An object from the photos and one of the same kind in OpenStreetMap less than 5 m apart count as one object, and each names the other. An object the software has found in no photo since 2023 becomes a checkpoint, a case set aside for a closer look.

title: How S6 is built and tested
section: The street each object stands on
text:
The street each object stands on
Each object belongs to the nearest S1 segment, a stretch of street, within 30 m. An object farther away has no street and says why: most are trees in parks, or benches and tables along the canal path. The stress test below shows that the distance only decides whether an object has a street, never which one.

title: How S6 is built and tested
text:
Width of a sidewalk
The city draws sidewalks as outlines and gives no width. S6 estimates a mean width as twice the area divided by the perimeter. This is exact for a long thin strip and a little low for short pieces. The typical (median) piece is about 2.3 m wide. A piece wider than 10 m on average would be listed for a look, since it is more likely a plaza or a joined drawing; none is.

Nine checks
Each check asks one plain question of what S6 wrote. Seven must pass, and all seven do; the last two only report.









Question
Answer




T1
Is every tree, hydrant, piece of furniture, OpenStreetMap point, road work, sidewalk and island here exactly once?
yes, 2,898 objects and 519 surfaces


T2
Does every object, and the centre of every surface, lie inside the study area?
yes


T3

yes; 196 trees without a planting date stay empty


T4

yes; 156 stand farther, each with its reason


T5

yes


T6

yes; 1,035 detections make 900 objects


T8

T9
How often do Mapillary’s detections stand within 5 m of an object a person recorded?
report: hydrants 68 of 82, crossings 74 of 102, cameras 2 of 34









TipTesting the tests



T5 failed on its first run. S6 measured each sidewalk from its full-precision outline, then stored the outline rounded to the centimetre, so the stored outline gave a slightly different area. S6 now measures the outline it stores.




Stress tests
Run twice on the same input, S6 gives the same output (X1). X2 changes the link distance. At 10 m, 644 objects have no street; at 20 m, 294; at 30 m, 156; at 50 m, 75. No object ever moves to another street, so the distance decides only how far an object may stand from its street. Of the 75 objects still without one at 50 m, 39 are benches, tables, bins and racks, and 28 are street lights, most likely in parks or along the canal. The other 8 are park trees.
X3 changes the distance within which detections of one kind become one object, from none to 8 m. Lights go from 877 to 628 and crossings from 111 to 73, while cameras barely change. The number of lights depends on this rule more than on anything else in S6. The matches with OpenStreetMap hold up to 5 m, then fall a little.

title: How S5 is built and tested
text:
From quarter-hours to hours
The city counts in 15-minute slices, by kind of road user. S5 keeps every slice counted within 15 m of an S1 junction, the same rule as the counts page. It adds them up by mode, keeping people on foot and bicycles apart from motor vehicles of every kind. A slice with nobody in it stays a counted zero, which differs from a slice nobody counted.
An hour gets a value only when all four of its quarters were counted. Several one-day windows open or close on the half hour, so their edge hours are partial. Sixteen hours at the junctions, 48 rows across the modes, stay empty, each noting how many quarters it had. S5 never stretches part of an hour into a whole one.

title: How S5 is built and tested
text:
The day’s shape
A busy junction and a quiet one can share a rhythm, so S5 compares each day with itself. The reference hours are those counted in full on every day: 7h, 8h, 11h, 12h, 16h and 17h. For each mode, each day is divided by its own mean over those six hours, so 1.0 is an ordinary daytime hour of that day. Two of the six fall in each of the city’s windows, so no window outweighs another.
A weekday hour takes the mean of every day that counted it, and keeps their lowest and highest values. Each value names the days behind it, so it can be rebuilt by hand. Outside the reference hours, most hours rest on J040 alone, and S5 marks them.
Only Tuesdays to Thursdays were counted. S5 lets their shape stand in for Monday and Friday, and says so on every such row. Saturday and Sunday stay empty, with the reason.

title: How S5 is built and tested
text:
Bicycle detectors
The city’s permanent bicycle detectors report every hour, for each site by direction and lane. S5 keeps the detectors that stand inside the study area, by the same test S4 uses for buildings: Peel at Ottawa, northbound and southbound, and William at Nazareth, westbound. Two detectors on Peel at Notre-Dame stand 35 and 49 m from junction J187, outside the area. S5 lists them without using them.
A recorded hour of 0 stays 0, and a missing hour is a gap. A detector’s day counts only when all 24 hours were recorded. The Griffintown day adds up the three detectors on the days when every one is complete: 376 days. Each such day is divided by its own mean over the same reference hours as the counts, then grouped by season and by kind of day (weekday, Saturday, Sunday). A group keeps its mean and its middle half, the range of the central half of its days.
The seasons follow whole months, as weather services count them: winter is December to February, spring is March to May, and so on. Holidays are not set apart, so a public holiday on a Monday counts as a weekday.

title: How S5 is built and tested
text:
The ring
A counted intersection joins the ring when it lies outside the study area and within 600 m of its edge. It must also stand more than 15 m from any S1 junction, the distance within which a count belongs to S1. S5 reads its quarter-hours and hours by the same rules as inside, and keeps each site’s mean per hour with weekdays and weekends apart. The ring feeds no shape or table S5 builds, and a test checks this.

title: How S5 is built and tested
text:
Reading opening hours
OpenStreetMap writes hours in a small grammar, like Mo-Fr 07:00-22:00; Sa 08:00-20:00; Su off. S5 reads the part of it Griffintown’s places use. A rule after a semicolon replaces what earlier rules said about the same days; a rule after a comma adds to them. A day the text never names is closed, which is the tag’s own convention. Hours past midnight carry into the next morning, so a bar open 17:00-03:00 on Saturday is open early on Sunday.
An opening with no closing time leaves those hours unknown. So does a note such as “sur rdv” (by appointment), or a text S5 cannot parse. Public holidays are set aside, since S5 has no calendar yet.
The city’s list of public places gives its hours in French, day by day, and sometimes for one season: the play fountains at Place des Aiguilleurs open from 21 May and close from 22 September. S5 keeps the season with the place.
A place counts as open in an hour when it is open at half past. A place with no hours is unknown at every hour, and S5 never marks it closed.

title: How S5 is built and tested
text:
Tests

Fourteen checks
Each check asks one plain question of what S5 wrote. Twelve must pass, and all twelve do; T11 and T12 only report. The Lab shows the latest results.









Question
Answer




T1
Does the evidence hold every counted quarter-hour, with the same totals as the city’s file?
yes, 1,440 quarters


T2
Does an hour get a value only when all four quarters were counted?
yes; 48 partial hours stay empty


T3
Were the reference hours counted every day, and does each day average 1 over them?
yes


T4
Can every hour of the weekday shape be rebuilt from the days it names?
yes


T5
Do Saturday and Sunday stay empty, with the reason?
yes


T6
Is every S4 place here once, and is a place without readable hours unknown at every hour?
yes, 610 rows: 558 places and 52 repeats, each pointing to its twin


T7
Does the hours reader give the expected week on fixed examples?
yes, 16 examples


T8
Does every place’s week come from its own hours text, and do the counts per hour add up?
yes


T9
Do the detector days hold every recorded hour, with a total only when all 24 were recorded?
yes; 309 incomplete detector-days have no total


T10
Can every bicycle shape and monthly level be rebuilt from the detector hours?
yes, 376 days


T11
How much do the sources cover?
report: 17 of 24 weekday hours rest on J040 alone; 83 of 558 places give hours


T12
Do the counts and the detectors agree on a weekday’s bicycles?
report: correlation 0.87 in winter, 0.89 over all seasons


T13
Is the ring every counted intersection outside the area within 600 m, at no S1 junction, and kept out of what S5 builds?
yes, 23 sites


T14
Can every hour of the ring be rebuilt from the city’s file, with weekdays and weekends apart?
yes









TipTesting the tests



A test that always passes proves nothing. So I broke the finished files five ways: I gave Saturday at 8h a value, turned one unknown hour of a place without hours into closed, added one person to one counted hour, filled a partial hour, and changed one letter of a place’s week in the Lab’s copy. Each was caught: the first by T4 and T5, the second by T6 and T8, the third by T1 and T4, the fourth by T1 and T2, and the last by the Lab’s check L7. Then I put the files back.




Stress tests
Run twice on the same input, S5 gives the same output (X1). The other stress tests ask how much the shape depends on so few days.
X2 leaves out one counted day at a time. In the reference hours, which all nine days share, no value moves by more than 0.12, and for people on foot and cars by no more than 0.06. In the hours J040 holds alone, its three December days disagree more. Leaving one out moves people on foot by up to 0.12 and bicycles by up to 0.44, since a few cyclists in an hour make a large share. The bicycle values at night and in mid-afternoon are the weakest numbers in S5.
X3 leaves out one junction at a time. The busiest hour stays 17h for every mode, with one exception: without J040, the bicycles’ busiest hour moves to 8h. So the evening cycling peak leans on J040.
X5 leaves out one month of detector days at a time. Weekday shapes hold well, moving by at most 0.05 in summer and 0.04 in autumn. Weekend shapes rest on fewer days and move more, up to 0.46 for a winter Sunday. Spring is the thinnest season, with 22 weekdays, 8 Saturdays and 9 Sundays.
X4 changes what “open in this hour” means. Of the other readings I tried, the strictest, open for the whole hour, removes 75 of the week’s 5,626 open place-hours, and the others move fewer. The choice of half past hardly matters.

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
The sources







Source
What S4 takes from it




OpenStreetMap, with its building parts
building outlines and tags, including tower parts with their storeys; places such as shops and cafés, with opening hours


Ville de Montréal, tax roll (Unités d’évaluation foncière), also with lot outlines (October 2026)
each property’s use, storeys, dwellings, year built and floor area, and the land it sits on


Ville de Montréal, Adresse ponctuelle
where each street number stands


Ville de Montréal, Locaux commerciaux et statuts d’occupation
every ground-floor commercial space in 2025, occupied or vacant


Ville de Montréal, Lieux et bâtiments à vocation publique
public places and their opening hours


Situ S1
the streets people can walk on



The city’s files are open under CC BY 4.0, and OpenStreetMap under ODbL.
The Concordia NGCI building file gives a height and a use for every building in Montréal. It carries no licence, though, so S4 does not use it. I publish nothing made from it until a licence is granted. It also records a condo tower such as 2199 rue Ann, 76 m tall, as one dwelling. Québec City’s building file does not cover Montréal. The city’s 3D model of 2020 (Bâtiments 3D 2020) measures roofs. It leaves out Le Sud-Ouest, Griffintown’s borough, and holds only three small structures by Rue Notre-Dame, at the edge of the study area (verified). The city’s 2016 model of Le Sud-Ouest predates most towers here, and I have not used it yet.

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
The outlines
Only OpenStreetMap draws buildings. Every other source is a list of points or rows. So S4 starts from its outlines and keeps each one whose centre falls inside the study area. When the centre of one outline lies inside a larger one, S4 treats the smaller as part of the larger. Griffix on Rue Wellington is an example: a 21-storey tower drawn over a 2-storey base.

title: How S4 is built and tested
section: The tax roll at its address
text:
The tax roll at its address
S4 matches each property’s street name and number to the city’s address points. Many rows found no match. I had downloaded the roll for whole streets across the island, and the address points only around Griffintown. I once thought none of the missed rows stood in the study area. The lot outlines showed that 64 do, and they now count through their lot.

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
Every row finds its building
The city also publishes the roll with the outline of each property’s lot, the land it is taxed on. Every condo unit repeats its lot. An address point is a single dot placed near a door or a curb, so a lot is firmer ground. S4 reads the lot first.
The buildings on a lot are those whose centre it holds. Failing that, any building covering at least 30% of the lot counts. When the lot holds one building, the row goes there. When it holds several, the address point says which. If the point stands in none of them, the nearest building within 15 m takes the row. When the lot holds no building, the address point works alone in the same way. Beyond 15 m a row stays unplaced, with the reason, since a longer reach risks the wrong building (stress tests).
Lot and point sometimes disagree. On a lot with one building, the lot decides. On a lot with several, where the point stands in a building off the lot, the point decides, since the lot cannot choose. Each such case becomes a checkpoint, a case flagged for me to look at by hand. There are ten so far.
Griffix is why the lot comes first. Its 197 flats, at 1045 rue Wellington, have their address point inside MaryRobert next door. S4 used to count them there, though their lot holds Griffix alone. Now they count in Griffix, and MaryRobert drops from 678 dwellings to 491.

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
The use
Each property’s land-use code begins with a digit naming a broad family, such as residential or commerce. A building takes the commonest family among its properties, leaving out condo parking spaces and storage units. A tie goes to the larger floor area, and a missing area is never read as zero. When the roll cannot decide, the OpenStreetMap tag speaks. A plain “building” tag names no use, so then the use stays empty, with the reason. Every tie goes on my list to check, because it often means two buildings share one outline. At Ardent Mills, for example, a 74-dwelling social housing property shares the flour mill’s outline.

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
Size
A building is as tall as its tallest known part. S4 takes the largest storey count from the roll or from OpenStreetMap, where every part inside the outline counts too, and notes the source. Condo units are left out, since the roll gives each only its own floor. I added the parts after an audit found MaryRobert at 2 storeys, because its outline carried only the podium. It now reads 22, from its tower. Where the dwellings cannot fit and no part helps, the building goes on my list to check. A building’s dwellings are the roll’s dwellings summed over its properties.

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
Ground floor and places
The premises are the 2025 survey’s spaces inside the building, vacant ones included. The places are anywhere a person might go. Some come from OpenStreetMap, and the rest from the city’s public places and the survey’s occupied shops. Benches and bike racks are left out. A survey shop and an OpenStreetMap shop with exactly the same name in the same building become one place. A looser match, like Orangetheory Fitness against Orangetheory Theory, would be a guess, so S4 leaves it alone.

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
The access link
S4 links each building to the nearest S1 street people can walk on, within 80 m, to stand in for the door. Every building’s record marks this link as the weakest value in S4.

title: How S4 is built and tested
text:
Tests

The checks
Each check asks one plain question of the finished buildings.







Question
Answer




Does every outline appear once, as a building or as part of one?
Yes: 296 buildings, and one tower drawn over its podium


Does every value name its source, and every empty one its reason?
Yes


Can every count be rebuilt from the source files?
Yes


Is every property and shop in one building or listed as unplaced, never twice?
Yes


Does each use follow its rule, ties included?
Yes


Is every building linked to a walkable street within 80 m, or does it say why not?
Yes. Six links are longer than 30 m, and Hangar 1825 has none


Is every place in or next to its building, with each shop listed twice pointing to its twin?
Yes, with 52 such pairs


Is any building lower than its tallest known part?
No. Nine take their storeys from a tower part


Does every property sit where its lot or address point puts it, with a checkpoint when the two disagree?
Yes



One more check reports how much the sources cover. A gap there is a fact about the sources, and it never counts as a failure. The Lab shows the latest results.


What the checks changed
The property check failed on its first run. 89 properties were counted twice, because the tax roll came in overlapping pages. S4 now keeps one row per property.
On the first map of uses, Ardent Mills, the flour mill, was painted residential. The roll puts a residential and an industrial property in its outline. My first rule broke the tie by the order of a list, a choice I never made on purpose. Ties now follow the floor-area rule in the use.
The height check came from an audit. I set MaryRobert back to 2 storeys, and the check named it at once, since one of its parts has 22. The same audit found an error in the arithmetic. Map coordinates run into the millions of metres, and at that size some outline centres lost their small digits. They fell tens of metres off, enough to put four small outlines falsely inside their neighbours. S4 now measures each outline from its own first corner, and the false overlaps are gone.






TipTesting the tests



A test that always passes proves nothing. So I broke the finished buildings file four ways. I removed the reason from an unknown use, added one dwelling to a building, changed one use that came from the roll, and wrote 0 into an empty dwelling count. The checks caught all four. I did the same to the Lab’s copy of the results, which a further check compares with S4 down to every outline point. I turned an unknown dwelling count to 0, changed one use, moved one point by 1 m and dropped one place. That check caught all four too.




Stress tests
Run twice on the same input, S4 gives the same output, line for line. The other stress tests ask how much the result depends on my choices.
The 15 m reach lets a stray address point join the nearest building. It matters a lot at first, then very little. With no reach, 1,322 rows would be left out. At 15 m, 468 are, and 415 of them sit at the one address point of checkpoint B01. At 30 m, two more find a building, and no property moves to another.
The last test shakes every address point by 2 m, then 5 m, as if the city had placed them a little off. At 2 m, 244 properties change building, and at 5 m, 278. The total stays at 11,954 dwellings. An earlier run gave 625 at 5 m. Part of the reason was that each point’s random move depended on the order the points were read in, so adding the lots reshuffled every move. Each point now has its own fixed move. Without lots the test gives 291 at 5 m, so the lots barely change this number (verified). Most properties sit on lots with several buildings, where the address point still decides.
That result is the warning. All the units at one address point move together. So where two buildings share a wall, a point a little off carries a whole condo tower into its neighbour. A single building’s count can be wrong while the block’s total is right. S5 and S7 should read dwellings by block, or with that in mind.

I gather the signs Mapillary detected within 30 m of the junction (getting the signs). Each sign has two readings of where it faces. One is Mapillary’s own angle, which I tested on stop signs. The other is the photo: if I can read a sign’s face, it is turned towards the camera. I call a decision likely when both readings point to the same street and the photo shows a sign that fits. I leave it open when the readings disagree, or when the photo does not show which way the sign faces. A sign newer than every photo stays open too.

title: S3 checks with photos
text:
What the photos showed
The photos settled the last turn-sign contradiction and all four no-entry disagreements. A photo now explains six no-entry signs, and the places to check fell from 27 to 21.

Wellington and Ann (J006)



J006. Each photo with what Mapillary read and the street that reading points to. Photos: Mapillary, CC BY-SA 4.0.


This was the last place where S3’s turn signs contradicted each other. The photos show three streets, each with its own sign. The green “straight only” on the west corner, seen in May 2022 and December 2023, faces Wellington arriving from the west (P01, likely). S3 had given it to the short split piece of Wellington, which caused the contradiction. The “left or right only” under the viaduct faces Rue Ann from the north (P02, likely). Mapillary read the green sign as its opposite, “no straight through”. So the photo decides, and the label alone never does.
One question stays open (P03). In 2024 a “straight only” sign stood under the viaduct, facing the short split piece of Wellington. In October 2025 the city installed a new post there with a stop and “left or right only”. No photo is newer, so S3 follows the city post and keeps the question on the list.


End of Brennan (J189)



J189. The end of Brennan in May 2024. Photos: Mapillary, CC BY-SA 4.0.


Bollards cross the street, and the no-entry signs at them close the paved area beyond to cars (P04, likely). The city file is right that cars may drive up to the bollards. The paving continues past them, which fits S1’s assumption C04 that walkers carry on. This does not show where the paving leads, though, so C04 stays an assumption.


East end of Bassins (J122)



J122. The east end of Rue des Bassins. Photos: Mapillary, CC BY-SA 4.0.


The no-entry sign hangs under a stop sign. Mapillary’s angle points within 2° of the path into the new park, so the sign closes the park to cars (P05, likely). Rue des Bassins itself stays two-way, as the city file says.


Notre-Dame and Inspecteur (J045)



J045. The corner of Notre-Dame and Inspecteur. Photos: Mapillary, CC BY-SA 4.0.


The two readings disagree, so the photo alone would leave this open. OpenStreetMap settles it. It draws Inspecteur north of Notre-Dame as two one-way halves, and the sign guards the half coming towards Notre-Dame (P07, likely). The city’s single two-way line is coarser. That is fine for S1, which works at the scale of whole streets.


Still open



J146. The park path off Rue William. Photos: Mapillary, CC BY-SA 4.0.


At the park path off William (P06), the two readings are far apart. The photos show the signs without showing which way they face. Two more no-entry signs, at the park connectors (J145), stand on recent posts that no photo shows. These stay open, along with P03 at Wellington and Ann.

title: S3 checks with photos
text:
Limits
Most of the photos come from the city’s own survey car, taken from 2022 to 2024. So a sign installed after the last photo cannot be checked this way. Mapillary’s labels and angles are only a first guess: one label said the opposite of the sign, and at J045 the two readings disagreed. Each decision is mine. It records how sure I am and why, so anyone can look at a sheet and disagree with it.

title: S2 Scores
text:
What S2 does
S2 attaches space syntax values to every S1 segment, and records the analysed line behind each value. Space syntax, begun by Bill Hillier and Julienne Hanson at University College London, measures where each street sits in the whole street network (what space syntax is). Integration is roughly how easy a street is to reach. Choice is roughly how often it lies on the way between other places. Both are measured within a radius, from 200 m up to the whole island.
S3 to S8 never read these values. Only S9 Observer uses them, at the very end, as a measuring stick (why).

title: S2 Scores
text:
Result

257 of 264 segments with walking values · 227 with vehicle values


Counts: S1 segments that received space syntax values: walking values from the island’s walking network, vehicle values from the driving network. Both come from PlanX runs of October 2026, whose version I did not record.
Does not show: that the values describe how people move. The 37 segments closed to cars get no vehicle value, by rule.

Almost every segment found its street exactly. 251 match one analysed line, and six lie over two pieces of the same street, such as Rue des Seigneurs and Rue Wellington. The seven without a walking value are Autoroute 10 and its ramps, which the walking network leaves out.
The 37 segments without a vehicle value should have none. They are paths and connectors, or streets closed to cars, such as the Allées or the pedestrian ends of Murray and Smith. Before October, 31 of them had one, because the older Sample 4 vehicle analysis included pedestrian ways.



How each segment was matched. Grey: a clean match. Pink: the exceptions, numbered and explained in the key.

title: S2 Scores
text:
What changed in October
On 10 October I reran both analyses on the rebuilt networks. Inside Griffintown the order of streets barely moved. I measured this with Spearman’s rank correlation, where 1.00 means no street changed place. It was 0.99 or 1.00 for every measure I compared.
Two changes are real, and both come from my own decisions. Rue Brennan and Rue Ann gained walking choice (the east end of Brennan from 0.00 to 0.90, Ann from 0.37 to 0.93), because I assumed they connect to the paths beyond them. If a photo shows these streets really stop, I will reject those decisions and the values will fall back. Murray and Smith lost vehicle choice. The driving network leaves out their pedestrian ends, by the same road rule S1 uses, so cars can no longer pass through there.
Values from different networks are different measurements. So the older Sample 4 values stay for reference and are never mixed with these.

title: S2 Scores
text:
Maps
The maps show four of the 13 values S2 holds for every street: walking at 800 m (about a ten-minute walk) and driving at 2000 m (a short trip by car). I chose these radii. 400 to 800 m is the usual low radius in space syntax studies (van Nes & Yamu 2021, p. 65), and Hillier, Yang and Turner (2012, p. 165) found 2000 m often significant in city work. Neither source ties 2000 m to cars, and neither radius comes from Griffintown’s data.

title: S1 Streets
text:
What S1 does
S1 turns the city’s street lines into a network of segments and junctions, and records who may use each segment. Every later system walks or drives on this network, so it has to be right first. The rules I assumed decide who may walk or drive where. I check the result twice: against itself in the tests, and against the street, using photos, in Checks and decisions.

title: S1 Streets
text:
Words



A made-up street that shows every word S1 uses.


A segment is a piece of street between two junctions. A junction is where segment ends meet. Griffintown is part of the city, so S1 also keeps the streets just outside the boundary that touch the study area. I call them the edge. A gate is where the study area meets the edge. An exit is the far end of an edge street, where the city carries on. A dead end is a junction with only one segment that is neither a gate nor an exit. A one-way arrow shows the only direction cars may use; pedestrians may always walk both ways. A checkpoint, with an id starting with C, is a place where I doubted the data and decided from photos.
S1 starts from the city’s street lines, the same lines my space syntax analysis uses. Space syntax, begun by Bill Hillier and Julienne Hanson, describes where each street sits in the whole network. S2 attaches its values to S1. Every segment keeps the city’s own id, so any value can be traced back to its source.

title: S1 Streets
text:
Result

232 segments inside · 32 on the edge


Counts: S1 segments, the pieces of street between two junctions, inside the study area and on its edge. They come from the city’s Géobase as cut in Sample 4, with the paths and the decisions I checked on photos (Checks and decisions).
Does not show: how long or how busy the streets are. The number depends on where the junctions fall.

Before the checks, S1 had 190 segments and 12 dead ends. Now it has 2 dead ends. A road map is a poor walking map. The city’s file left out the canal path and the new park paths, and 10 of the 12 dead ends turned out to be places where walkers continue.

What changed in October
The October rebuild came from decisions about the boundary and a few street ends. Every segment and junction that existed before kept its number.
The boundary was a drawing decision. The city draws Boulevard Robert-Bourassa as two one-way roads about 60 m apart. The boundary ran between them, so inside the study area the boulevard carried traffic one way only. S1 now takes in both carriageways (C19) and keeps the edge around the whole area.
At the street ends, the Lachine Canal path (C16) and two park paths (C18) came in for walkers. A footway now runs from the end of Brennan through the block to de la Commune (C04, C12), and the end of Ann joins it (C05). These links are assumed. They stay pink until a photo or a visit confirms them. From the end of Smith, a 41 m link crosses the plaza of Place des Aiguilleurs (C06). Photos settled that one.

title: S1 Streets
text:
From here to there
In the Lab, choose S1, then “from here to there”, and click a start and an end junction. Everything it shows comes from the network alone:







Measure
What it tells you




Shortest route
the shortest way along the streets, on foot or by car; the other measures compare against it


Directness
route length divided by the straight line; a grid gives about 1.3, and a barrier such as the canal pushes it higher


Variety
in blue, every street a trip could use if it were at most 0, 5, 10, 25 or 50 % longer than the shortest; a thin band means the layout funnels everyone onto one street


Cost of one-way streets
how much longer the drive is than the walk between the same two junctions



Choose “minutes on foot” and click anywhere near a street to see how far you can walk from there. Streets you reach within 5 minutes turn yellow, within 10 blue and within 15 violet, at an ordinary pace of 1.3 m a second; many people walk slower. The side lists the homes, places and stops in reach. Only the streets of the area are walked, so a place just past its edge may be closer than it looks.
From William at Young to further along William is 306 m on foot and 966 m by car. William is one-way, so the car has to go round the block. From Bassins at Rioux to Notre-Dame at Robert-Bourassa, a 10 % detour opens up 82 other segments: the grid gives walkers many ways. From Bassins at Allée des Barges to Wellington, the walk is 1.7 times the straight line, because the canal has few crossings.
These measures say nothing about how anyone actually chooses a route. People do not all take the shortest way, and the turn bans and stops of S3 are left out. Routes also stay inside the study area, so many car trips would need the city outside. The Lab says so when that happens. How people choose belongs to S9, which can measure any route it imagines against this yardstick. The Lab notes describe how the measures themselves are tested.

text:
The edge
People and cars cross the boundary, so S1 keeps the edge and applies the same rules there as inside, for walkers and for the direction of cars. The tests, and later the agents, assume the rest of the city can be reached from the exits. S3 reads the signs on the edge too, so a junction on the boundary sees every street that meets it. Later systems decide what to do with the edge: S4 puts no buildings there, and S9 measures inside the boundary only.

title: How S1 is built and tested
text:
Numbering
Pieces added by decisions after the October rebuild are numbered after everything else, the edge included. That way, confirming or rejecting one of them never changes another id.

title: How S1 is built and tested
text:
Joining an added path
Each end of an added path joins whatever is nearest within 25 m: a junction, or a street that gets cut at that spot. A junction wins if it is at most 5 m further away. A street dead end within 25 m of the middle of a path is joined to it too. That is how the Allées reach the canal. A decision taken from a photo may instead name the street to join, up to 60 m away.

title: How S1 is built and tested
text:
Two ideas behind it

Inside or outside?How far can I get?


To tell whether a point lies inside the study area, imagine a line running right from it and count how often it crosses the outline. An odd count means inside. This is called ray casting. S1 applies it to the halfway point of each segment.


Start at one junction and take every allowed move. Then take every move from each place you reached, and so on. This is called breadth-first search, and each round is one step. The reach view in the Lab plays it round by round.

title: Reading closely
text: Many sentences on this site lean on a book or a paper. In October I went back to each of those texts with the page open. I wanted to see whether my sentence still said what the author said. Most did. A few had drifted, usually by a small step, and always in the same direction: towards what my model needed the reading to say. Those few cases taught me the most.

title: Reading closely
text:
Where my sentences had drifted
I had written that people “tend to keep going roughly straight”, citing Hillier and Iida. Their claim is narrower. People judge routes by how much they turn (Hillier & Iida 2005, p. 476). That is about how people compare routes. It says little about what a walker does at each corner. The difference will matter when S7 gives walkers a way to choose their routes.
I had also written that 2000 m is a common radius for driving. Hillier, Yang and Turner call radius 2000 “safe to use” for cities in general (2012, p. 165). They say nothing about cars. Using it for driving is my choice, and the S2 page now says so.
A third sentence claimed that walkers who always take the route with the least turning would reproduce the choice values by construction. (Choice is how often a street lies on the way between other places.) That holds only if trips are spread evenly over every pair of places (Turner 2007, p. 544). Real trips are not. People go to work and to shops far more often than to a random corner. I added the condition.
The last case is about my own reading. My definition of a spatial culture, “a distinctive way of ordering space”, comes from Hillier (1989). I know it only through Griffiths and von Lünen’s quotation of it (2016, p. xxiii). I have kept it, and I say plainly that it is second-hand.

title: Reading closely
section: What held, and what it leaves open
text:
What held, and what it leaves open
The claim the whole method rests on did hold. Hillier and his colleagues found that the layout of the street network is “the main generator of patterns of movement” (1993, p. 29). The same paper shows how much that depends on place. Across ten parts of King’s Cross, the correlation between layout and counted movement ranges from 0.25 to 0.80 (p. 46). Shops can also multiply movement beyond what the layout predicts (p. 31). Ratti (2004) adds that the results shift with how the map is drawn. Together these are my reason for keeping space syntax out of the simulation and using it only as a measuring stick.

title: Reading closely
section: Checking the software against the papers
text:
Checking the software against the papers
PlanX, the QGIS plugin I use for the analysis, follows the published measures. Two details matter before comparing its numbers with other studies.

Does PlanX count a journey once, or once each way?
PlanX’s manual leaves this open, and its own output answers it. Take a street segment that leads into a dead end and meets only two other lines at its far end. Every journey from the dead end passes through it, and no other journey does. So its choice value is simply the number of those journeys. In 103 such cases, PlanX’s value counts each pair of places once, and never gives the doubled number. So PlanX counts each pair once, as Turner defines choice (2007, p. 544). A tool that counted both ways would give somewhat higher normalised choice values (assumption). That matters before comparing Griffintown with a published study.


Which NAIN?
For normalised choice (NACH), PlanX reproduces the published formula exactly. For normalised integration (NAIN), the paper gives one form in its text and another in its appendix. PlanX uses a third.



Form
Where it appears
Matches PlanX




NC^1.2 / TD
the paper’s text, p. 165
no


(NC + 2)^1.2 / TD
the paper’s appendix, p. 191
no


(NC + 2)^1.2 / (TD + 2)
PlanX
yes



The three forms rank the streets almost identically, so the maps do not change. The numbers themselves differ, so compare a NAIN from this site only with one computed the same way.
As a last check, Hillier, Yang and Turner (2012, p. 162) report that real cities have a mean NACH between about 0.7 and 1.2. Montréal on my walking network has 0.80. This suggests the network was built and analysed in an ordinary way.

title: Reading closely
text:
Still to read
Decoding the City by Offenhuber and Ratti (2014) will matter once the project turns to images and video of the street. The Depthmap handbook and manual will matter when I compare PlanX with Depthmap. Where this site cites Lefebvre’s Rhythmanalysis and the archival readings, the page numbers sit beside each quotation.
Close reading tells me whether a sentence matches its source. Whether the source is right is a separate question. Several of these readings are still debated, and I try to say so where I use them.

title: From systems to a game
text:
The systems describe Griffintown. A game needs them for four jobs: a world to stand in, people moving through it on time, places where something can happen, and a way to check the result. Each system does one of these jobs first. This page says which, with the counts each system holds today.
I treat the move from a system to the game as a translation. A system is the source. Each decision that turns part of it into a game element is written down, with its kind (source observation, researcher decision, assumption or gap) and an alternative. The first part of that translation is built: G1 World (verified). The rest is planned.

section: What no system gives the game
text:
What no system gives the game
Two kinds of knowledge are missing from every system. Griffintown in the 1920s to 1940s needs historical maps and records. What residents know needs interviews and focus groups, after research ethics approval. Until then, the game can hold Griffintown’s present layout and its weekday commute, and every other part of its rhythm is an assumption the ledger names.

title: Limits of the desk
text: So far I have built Situ from open data: files that public bodies or volunteers publish for anyone to use, such as the city’s tax roll or OpenStreetMap. I have seen Griffintown mostly through other people’s photos and videos. I have not yet checked this desk research by walking the area with a notebook, and that limits what every system can claim.

title: Limits of the desk
text: So far I have built Situ from open data: files that public bodies or volunteers publish for anyone to use, such as the city’s tax roll or OpenStreetMap. I have seen Griffintown mostly through other people’s photos and videos. I have not yet checked this desk research by walking the area with a notebook, and that limits what every system can claim.

title: Limits of the desk
text:
Where the files fall short
The first limit is purpose. Each file was made by an institution to do a job, and its categories serve that job. Scholars of data say the same: data are shaped for a purpose before anyone analyses them (Gitelman 2013; Kitchin 2014). When I borrow a file for a new question, its categories come with it.
The city’s street file is a road file. It left out the canal path and the new park paths, and 10 of the first 12 dead ends in S1 turned out to be places where walkers carry on. The tax roll is for taxing property. It counts a condo parking space as a property, just as it counts a home, and gives a tower’s storeys only for some kinds of property.
The second limit is time. Every file has its own date, and Griffintown changes faster than most of them. The city’s sign post at one corner under the Wellington viaduct dates from October 2025, while every photo of it is older (P03). The city’s 3D model of 2020 stops at the Ville-Marie borough line. Griffintown is in Le Sud-Ouest, so it only has the 2016 model, older than many of its towers. When two files disagree, the cause is often a gap in time.
The third limit is coverage. The speed file has no limits for Autoroute 10 and its ramps. The traffic light file says where the lights are and nothing about their timing. No open file says where building doors are. OpenStreetMap is drawn by volunteers, so a building appears only once someone draws it.
The fourth limit is position. A point in a file stands for a thing on the street, and the two are rarely in the same spot. An address point often sits at the curb, a shop’s point on its façade. At 1485 rue des Bassins, 290 dwellings share one address point, 130 m from the two towers on their lot (B01). Even my own arithmetic can move things: an early version of S4 put some building centres tens of metres off, because of how it handled large map coordinates.

title: Limits of the desk
text:
Seeing from the desk
Photos and videos let me look at the street without being there. They settled real questions, including most of the no-entry disagreements in S3. Mapillary photos from 2016 and 2024 showed that walkers cross Place des Aiguilleurs at the end of Rue Smith (C06). A walking video filmed on 11 July 2026 shows the signs at the entrance of Allée des Vraquiers: a pedestrian zone, closed to bicycles and to every vehicle except emergency ones.
Still, a camera goes where its owner walks, and it records one moment. Neither of the two recent walking videos reaches the end of Rue Brennan, so the footway I assumed there (C04) is still unconfirmed. A sign seen edge-on hides which street it faces. A photo older than the sign it shows can mislead.
So every decision keeps its source and its date, and I grade the evidence. A link I assume is drawn in pink. A photo or video can make it likely. Only a visit makes it confirmed. Videos are cited by link and timestamp, and no frame appears here unless its owner agrees.

title: Limits of the desk
text:
People are missing
The deepest limit is about people. Open data records a city’s infrastructure. Apart from the city’s movement counts at a few intersections (Movement counts) and its bicycle detectors, it says almost nothing about how people use the streets: where they linger, or when a corner fills. Situ aims to mediate and archive Griffintown’s urban rhythm and its spatial culture, which Hillier described as a distinctive way of ordering space (About). Both live in what people do. From the desk I can describe the stage. I cannot yet describe the play.

title: Limits of the desk
text:
Carrying the gaps
A value no source gives stays empty, with the reason written beside it. It never becomes a zero or a guess. Every assumption is labelled as one on the page and in the Lab. Every place the desk could not settle becomes a checkpoint: a question to answer on site.
So Situ describes Griffintown as its files and other people’s cameras record it, at dates I can name. It shows how the layout and the rules shape the movement that is possible. How people actually live in the area is still beyond it. Each system says which of the two it is doing.
Most remaining checkpoints can only be closed on site. The next step is a walk through Griffintown with these questions in hand, photographing and dating each answer. Later, watching people in place will add to S5 Rhythm, the first system about time, which so far knows only weekdays.

title: Lab notes
text:
The Lab is one map with a tab for each system. There I try a system and see the places it still leaves open. Click anything to see what every system knows about it.
The Lab replays results. It never recomputes them. Every street colour and slider position shows something a system already wrote down: the reach slider, for instance, steps through how far S1 found you can get from a junction. So each rule lives in one place, and the Lab cannot quietly disagree with it.
Routes are the one small exception. Storing every route between every pair of junctions would take many megabytes. So I store only the shortest distances and the last step of each shortest route. The browser follows each route back and tests each street against the detour allowed. Those two rules exist twice, beside the systems and in the browser, and a test runs both on 45,600 cases to check they give the same streets.

Two orders on one map
Two views put two measures on the same street. In S2, “local or whole” compares a street’s place within 200, 400 or 800 m with its place across the whole island. In S9, “against space syntax” compares a street’s place among the imagined walkers with its place in walking choice or integration. A street’s place runs from 0, the lowest, to 1, the highest; the view shows the first place minus the second. Yellow means higher in the first order, blue higher in the second, grey about the same, and the line widens with the gap. Python works out the gaps (common/ranks.py) and the Lab only draws them; check L13 counts them again a different way.
The gaps describe the data. Why a street is high in one order and low in the other is a question for the pages and for fieldwork (assumption).

title: Movement counts and light timing
section: Estimating the lights with Webster’s method
text:
Estimating the lights with Webster’s method
S3 knows where the 31 lights in S1 are. The city does not publish their timing, so the timing is my estimate.
Webster’s method (Webster 1958) is the classic way to set a fixed light cycle from counted traffic. A cycle is one full round of greens. The method asks how full each approach is, and which cycle length keeps the delay smallest. I apply it to the busiest counted hour.
An approach’s load is the cars arriving per hour (a bus or truck counts as two) divided by what its lanes can pass while green. Each lane, counted from OpenStreetMap, passes about 1,800 cars an hour. Each phase (one turn of green) takes the load of its fullest approach, and the phases add up to a total load. Webster’s formula turns that load, and the time lost each time the green changes (4 s per phase here), into a cycle length. Each phase then gets green in proportion to its load. I add one check Webster does not make. A pedestrian crossing needs at least 7 s to start, plus the time to cross at 1.2 m/s. A shorter green is lengthened.
The two phases follow the street grid: north-south, then east-west. Grid north is at about 305° on the compass, as in the city’s counts. At J040 almost nothing arrives from the north, where Ottawa is the one street no car may arrive along. That confirms the orientation.



The estimated cycles, second by second. Grey is amber and all-red: the time lost when the green changes.


At J040, at 16h on 18 December 2024, the total load was 0.29 and Webster’s cycle came to 24 s. At J051 the load was 0.38 and the cycle 27 s. Traffic is far from filling these lights, and both cycles are much shorter than any city would use, so I apply my lower limit of 60 s. The green is then set by pedestrians and by the split of loads: 26 s each way at J040, and 38 s north-south against 14 s east-west at J051. That is a finding about Griffintown’s streets, and a warning. At these volumes traffic leaves the timing open, so it becomes a design choice.
J181, on Robert-Bourassa, is skipped. Three of its four approaches lie beyond the network, and Webster needs them all.

title: Movement counts and light timing
text:
The other 29 lights
I weighed four options. A single plan would give a main street and a side street the same green. Borrowing the split of a counted light on the same streets would use real counts, but only two lights were counted. Timing the lights from space syntax was ruled out, because S9 would then measure its own input. I chose to share the green by road class, the city’s own street hierarchy, which S1 already holds.
The city’s 2007 review of its arterial network (PDF) gives each class a daily traffic range: main arteries carry over 30,000 vehicles, collectors 1,000 to 15,000. Managing the flow is “prépondérante” on main arteries and “peu” on collectors (Ville de Montréal 2007). The United States standard agrees: “In general, the higher the traffic volume is, the higher the functional classification will be” (FHWA 2023, p. 26, PDF). Webster (1958) shares the green by how full each approach is, so a busier street should get more of it.
The counts agree. At all five counted junctions where the two streets differ in class, the higher class carried more traffic over the day. At J040, William, a collector, carried 2.5 times as much as Guy. Wellington, a secondary arterial, carried 8.5 to 29 times as much as Ann, Murray, Young and Shannon. Four of the five are on Wellington, so the sample is small.
At the two counted lights, road class and Webster disagree. At J040 it would give 21 and 31 s where Webster gives 26 and 26, because at the busiest hour each lane is about as full on both streets. At J051 it would give 26 and 26 s where Webster gives 38 and 14: the classes are equal, but de la Montagne is busier. So class tells which street gets more green over a day, and says nothing of how much at a given hour. The counted lights therefore keep Webster, and the share by class stays a cautious 60 %.
The rule: each street arriving at a light belongs to one of the two axes. Each axis takes the highest class among its streets, from main arterial (with highway) down through secondary arterial and collector to local. If both axes have the same class, the two phases share the 52 s of usable green equally. If not, the higher class gets 60 % and the lower 40 %. No phase is shorter than its pedestrians need, and where they need more, the cycle grows. Where cars arrive on one axis only, the other phase is for pedestrians.
Of the 31 lights, 2 follow Webster from counts, 17 have one street of higher class, 7 have equal classes, and 5 have cars on one axis only (mostly at the edge, where the cross street lies beyond the network). In S9 these become the light plans its imagined drivers stop at, with the 60 % share and the 60 s cycle written down as assumptions. The city’s pedestrian-signal file uses the same intersection numbers as its light file: 30 of the 31 lights have pedestrian signals, all but Seigneurs and William.

title: Movement counts and light timing
text:
Assumptions
Two numbers are mine alone. The 60 s lower limit on the cycle (120 s is the upper) is my guess for a city centre, and it sets every cycle here. The 60 % share is my choice too: the counts show which street is busier and say nothing of the amount. The other values (lane capacity, time lost per phase, walking speed and walk interval) follow Webster or common practice. Montréal publishes neither its amber and all-red times nor its walking speed. The OpenStreetMap lane counts cover 866 of 870 car ways, and I checked them at three junctions only.
The counts themselves cover a few days each, in winter or spring. They show those days. A typical year is beyond them.

title: About Situ
text:
Situ is the prototype for my PhD research-creation project. It asks whether a game-like 3D experience can pass on and archive the spatial culture and urban rhythm of Griffintown, Montréal. I look at two eras: today, and the 1920s to 1940s. I work from the city’s open data and from my own observation, and I read both through urban theory. Game design then carries the result to a player.
Nothing in Situ archives anything yet. What exists so far is a foundation: the street network with its rules and buildings, and the measures I will test it against.

title: About Situ
section: Research-creation: systems made for a game
text:
Research-creation: systems made for a game
Situ is research-creation: the research and the making answer each other. The research half is the systems. They hold what open data and photos say about Griffintown, with every source and gap in view, and each is tested before the next one uses it. The making half is the game, which is planned.
The systems are made to inform the game’s design. Each one prepares a part of Griffintown a game needs: the ground one can move on (S1), how that ground is laid out (S2), the rules of the road (S3), places to go (S4), the hours (S5), the objects in the street (S6), who commutes and when (S7), what can be seen (S8), and movement imagined from all of these (S9). Designing the game means reading each system as a source and translating it into rules and spaces. Playing it sends something back to the research: routes to compare with the counts and with space syntax, and questions to bring to residents.
From systems to a game sorts the systems by the job each does in a game: the world, the rhythm of the NPCs, the points where something can happen, and the check. The first step of that translation, G1 World, is built and tested. The rest is planned.

title: About Situ
text:
The idea

Spatial culture
Hillier described a spatial culture as “a distinctive way of ordering space” (Hillier 1989, quoted in Griffiths & von Lünen 2016, p. xxiii). Griffiths and von Lünen see the field as the link between how a built place works and what it comes to mean to the people who live there (2016, p. xxi). Adams (2024, introduction) wants spatial culture to be “qualified and documented”. That is close to what an archive needs.


Rhythm
A street layout holds no time. Space syntax is the method Hillier and Hanson started for measuring how a street network is arranged (What space syntax is). It tends to strip social practice of its time (Griffiths & von Lünen 2016, p. xxiii). In Rhythmanalysis, Lefebvre finds rhythm wherever energy is spent in a particular place and time (2004, p. 15). His own example is a Paris junction seen from his window: on red the pedestrians cross, on green the cars rush (p. 28). The light cycles in S3 model that beat. He also holds that where there is rhythm there is measure (p. 8), so counts and timings belong in Situ. I add time on purpose: when places are open and when streets are busy.


Archiving
An archive keeps two things (Schellenberg 1956, pp. 139 to 140). One is the evidence records give of how their maker worked. The other is the information they hold about people and places. Situ keeps both. The city data says what Griffintown is. My decision files and tests record how I turned it into a model. The London Charter, a set of principles for visualising cultural heritage by computer, calls this layer paradata (2009, principle 4.6). The Seville principles ask that a reconstruction show what is real and what is not (López-Menchero & Grande, principle 4), and that others can test it (principle 7). So every decision in my files carries a status, such as confirmed or assumed, and every claim on these pages carries one of four words.
Rhythm is the hard part. Taylor separates the archive of lasting things from the repertoire of embodied practice, like walking to work or lingering at a corner (2003, pp. 19 to 20). The repertoire needs people to be present. Situ cannot store a rhythm the way it stores a street. It can keep traces, such as counts and timings. It can also offer a place where the rhythm is performed again: the game. The Seville principles warn against showing “lifeless cities” (principle 5.3).


What Situ has and what it lacks
Lefebvre describes three moments of social space (1991, pp. 38 to 40). Each kind of source in Situ lines up with one of them, so I use them as a checklist. Every row is open to revision.



Lefebvre
In Situ

NoteFour readings I make, and how I defend them





These are my own interpretations of the sources. For each one I give the strongest objection I know, and what would show me wrong.

Lefebvre’s triad as a checklist
Lefebvre warns that his three moments lose their force once they become an abstract model (1991, p. 40). Laying them over software comes close to that. So I use the table only to see what is missing, and for now the lived row is empty. The rows also leak: the counts are observation, yet the city decided where to count. If the rows cannot be kept apart at all, the table should show where they cross.


Where layout and movement disagree
A gap between space syntax and observed movement points to something besides the layout, such as a shop or a rule. Griffiths and von Lünen ask research to spell out that kind of gap (2016, p. xxi). The 1993 paper on natural movement (the share of walking the layout alone produces) itself shows shops multiplying the layout’s effect (Hillier et al. 1993, p. 31). A difference may also be plain error, from a wrong network or too few counts. So it counts only after each system’s tests. The reading is wrong if the differences vanish once errors are fixed, or if they follow no pattern.


Schellenberg’s two values
Schellenberg drew his line between evidence and information from government records (1956, pp. 139 to 140, 148). A research model is no government agency. I borrow only the distinction, which he says he defines “quite arbitrarily” (p. 139), and the London Charter already carries it into visualisation. The borrowing fails if the two layers cannot be kept apart. So my corrections live in their own file, and the city’s files stay untouched.


The game as a place to perform rhythm again
Taylor’s repertoire and Lefebvre’s rhythm both need bodies present, and play is embodied action too. Against this, a player alone in a simulation receives no memory from Griffintown’s people. The game itself is code and data, an archive object. Lefebvre adds that the rhythmanalyst is closer to the poet than to “the statistician, who counts things” (2004, p. 23).
I accept most of this. The game keeps traces and sets up a new performance. It does not hold the original repertoire, so interviews and focus groups are in the plan. If players’ movement bears no relation to the recorded rhythms, the game performs nothing of Griffintown.






Space syntax as one measuring stick
Space syntax describes the layout. I use it only to measure, and the simulated walkers never read it. At the end, S9 compares where they went with what space syntax predicts and with the city’s counts. Where they agree, the layout may explain the movement. Where they differ, something else is at work, and that difference is what the archive should keep.

title: The walking network
text:
The city’s street file (Géobase) draws streets and leaves out most paths away from them. These include the Lachine Canal path and the park paths in Griffintown. Space syntax measures how each street sits within the whole network (what it is), so it reads the network all at once (why that matters). A missing path therefore does double harm. Its own place is empty, and the streets around it look less connected than they are.
Before running the analysis, I built one walking network for the whole island of Montréal, with the paths people actually use. My earlier analysis files (Sample 4) stay untouched beside it. Cars get their own network.

title: The walking network
text:
What changed

Taken outAdded


Highways come out, because nobody walks on them. So do streets that exist only as plans. Painted bike lanes and paths drawn on top of a street stay out, since the street is already there. Added pieces that join nothing are dropped, because a piece on its own would get meaningless values.


I added the off-street bike and multi-use paths from the city’s bike network, because people walk on them. That includes the separated paths on bridges, which the city files under a highway. I also added the two Griffintown park paths I checked on photos in S1 (decision C18). Sometimes a path end and a street do not quite touch in the data. There a short straight line joins them, which I call a connector. Every connector is listed.




47,197 lines


Counts: every line of the island’s walking network as PlanX analysed it: 46,041 pieces of city streets, 740 added path pieces and 416 connectors. They come from the city’s Géobase (its files are dated 17 September 2026) and its bike network, joined by my merge script on 10 October 2026 (merge report).
Does not show: how much anyone walks. A line is a piece of a file, and lines differ in length.

Of these, 740 are added path pieces (161 km in all) and 416 are connectors.
The network carries the same October decisions as S1: the footway behind Brennan and Ann (C04), and the link across Place des Aiguilleurs from the end of Smith (C06).

NoteEach step in plain words





A path counts as a duplicate when most of its length runs within 10 m of a street. Joining follows the S1 rules. A path end joins the nearest junction or street, and a street dead end may join the middle of a path. Across the island the gap may be at most 15 m. In Griffintown, and at places I have checked on a photo, it may be 25 m, because only there have I looked. A path that crosses a street with no junction stays unjoined, since it could be a bridge or a tunnel. Where a connector lands mid-street, the street is split there. Last, added pieces cut off from the main network are dropped; city streets never are.



Six checks follow. They confirm that every walkable city street is still there at its full length, and that no painted bike lane slipped in. Every connector is within its limit, and Griffintown matches S1. Two checks list what is left to look at: 73 places where an added path crosses a street with no junction, and six small parts cut off from the main network.

title: The walking network
section: The one gap I settled by hand: Île-des-Sœurs
text:
The one gap I settled by hand: Île-des-Sœurs
Île-des-Sœurs is not an example I picked. It is the one place where the merge’s own rules failed in a way that mattered. On the first run, the whole island was cut off from the rest of the network: the bike path from the bridge ends 15.2 m from the boulevard, just over the 15 m limit for joining a path to a street. The merge report lists every part cut off from the main network, and a whole neighbourhood stood out among them.
It matters for Griffintown only at radius n, where every street of the island counts. A neighbourhood left out would shift those values a little everywhere. At 200, 400 and 800 m it changes nothing in Griffintown, which lies more than 2 km away. Raising the limit for the whole island would have made joins everywhere else, so I checked this one place on a photo.



The path meets Boulevard de l’Île-des-Sœurs at a painted crossing. Photo: Sacha862, December 2024, via Mapillary (CC BY-SA 4.0).


The crossing is real. I recorded it as a checked place (M01), and the longer Griffintown limit now applies near it. Six small parts are still cut off, 58 lines in all: 48 of them around Avenue Ash, the rest private lanes and single streets. The city’s files give them no walkable link to the rest, so they keep values only within their own part (merge report, check C6). Outside Griffintown, Île-des-Sœurs is the only place I checked on photos.

title: The walking network
text:
Risks
Every added path is a claim about where people can walk. I want each one to carry its evidence, a dated photo that anyone can dispute. A connector could join two things that are separate in reality. That is why the gaps are short and every connector is listed. A real link could also stay unjoined, so the 73 crossings are listed for me to check one by one. Near Griffintown the risk is low: one unjoined crossing within 800 m, four within 2 km.
Bike paths stand in for footpaths, and a few may be unpleasant or closed to walking. So I took only separated paths and multi-use trails. The city maps park footpaths less well than bike paths, and I checked only Griffintown on photos. Values far from Griffintown are therefore less certain.

title: The walking network
text:
The analysis
On 10 October I ran PlanX 4.19.0, the QGIS tool that computes the values, with the Sample 4 pedestrian settings. That means angular segment analysis at radii of 200, 400 and 800 m and across the whole network. Every line kept its number and shape, so S2 can trace each value to one line. The first run that day used a faulty Smith link (C06) that joined Smith to itself (how it was found). The evening rerun, checked line by line, matches the network.

title: The walking network
text:
The driving network
The vehicle network starts from every city line. It leaves out the lines cars may not use under the S1 road classes, plus one small group of streets no car can reach. The rest stay exactly as the city drew them, highways included. Segment analysis reads every line as two-way, though one-way streets keep their direction in the data. I ran PlanX on it on 10 October, at radii of 1200 and 2000 m. The Sample 4 vehicle values came from a network that included pedestrian ways. Now no segment closed to cars carries a vehicle value (S2).
