A passing test says the code does what I meant. It says nothing about whether Griffintown works that way. So I keep three kinds of checking apart.

Implementation: does the code do what I meant? Each system’s tests and stress runs, checked again by the Lab. A test either passes or fails; a few only report a number, and the counts below leave those out.
Correspondence: do the results match something observed independently? Photos, or a second source such as the city’s counts.

title: How S2 is built and tested
text:
The problem
S1 and the walking network were built from the same city lines, and each cut them in its own places. S1 cuts where a park path joins a street. The walking network cuts wherever a bike path joins one. So an S1 segment and an analysed line are often the same street with different ends. Rue des Seigneurs is one S1 segment lying over two analysed pieces with different values. Matching by id alone would hide that. Matching by shape finds both.

title: How S2 is built and tested
text:
The matching rule



A made-up segment and the analysed lines under it.


I place a test point about every metre along each S1 segment. Each point looks for the closest analysed line within 1 m, but only among lines of the same kind. A city street looks only at pieces of the same street in the city’s records. A path or connector looks only at its own kind.
The cover is the share of the segment’s length that found a line. The value is the mean of the lines found, each weighted by the metres it shares with the segment. With one line, it is exactly that line’s value. With 95 % cover or more, the segment counts as matched, or as split when its value comes from two lines. Between 50 and 95 % it keeps its value and is marked partial, so the gap stays visible. Below 50 % it gets no value and a written reason. Today no segment is partial.
The same-kind rule matters near junctions. There, a test point at the end of a street also lies within 1 m of the crossing street. Without the rule, a street could take some of its neighbour’s values. The stress tests measure that risk.

title: How S2 is built and tested
text:
Vehicle values
The driving network keeps the city’s lines uncut. So every S1 piece of a street simply takes the vehicle value of the same city street id. First, S2 asks whether cars may use the street, by the same rule S1 uses. Streets closed to cars, and every added path or connector, are marked as not roads, with a written reason. A street open to cars and missing from the analysis would be marked missing. Today there are none.

title: How S2 is built and tested
text:
Tests

Checks
Each check asks a plain question of the result, and all of them pass. The Lab lists the latest run.







Question
Answer




Does every S1 segment have exactly one row?
Yes


Is a value present exactly when it should be, and is every missing value empty, with a reason?
Yes


Can every walking value be rebuilt from the trace of analysed lines behind it?
Yes


Is any value invented, or outside the values of its lines?
No


Do values come only from the same kind of line, and from the same street for city streets?
Yes


Do vehicle values equal the vehicle analysis for the same street?
Yes



A seventh check only reports coverage: the numbers under Result.






TipThe trace check caught a real problem



On the first run the trace check failed. The trace rounded the shared metres to two decimals, too coarse to rebuild the values exactly. I now store them to six.




Stress tests
The stress tests ask how easily the result could go wrong. Each one changes one thing on purpose and measures what moves.
Two runs on the same input give identical results. Any matching distance from 5 cm to 10 m gives the same result, and test points every 25 cm or every 5 m move a value by about 0.01 at most. Shaking every S1 point by up to 0.3 m changes one segment: a 15 m connector at Brennan, which then takes part of its value from the next connector. At 0.8 m, six segments change status, mostly paths and connectors along the canal, and no value moves by more than 0.08.
The test that matters most turns the same-kind rule off. With nothing shaken, no segment then takes values from another line. Shaken by 0.8 m, 142 segments do. The worst is the short Smith link, which moves by 0.24 as it takes values from the streets at both its ends.



As the S1 points are shaken further, segments without the same-kind rule start taking values from crossing streets. With the rule, almost nothing moves.


Today the match is exact because S1 and the walking network share coordinates, so the matching distance has no effect. If the geometry drifted, for example after someone edits S1 in QGIS, the same-kind rule would keep S2 honest.
The rule test also found a fault upstream. Before a fix, Rue Smith picked up 21 m from a connector lying on top of it. That was the C06 link, which joined Smith to its own other end. I fixed the rule in S1 (C06), and after the new PlanX run no such segment remains.

title: How S3 is built and tested
text:
Approaches
A sign speaks to drivers arriving from one direction, so S3 starts from the approaches. An approach is one segment end (a segment is one piece of S1 street), seen as a car drives towards the junction. For each one, S3 records the arriving car’s heading, whether the one-way rules let a car arrive or leave along it, the segment’s length, and whether the junction is an exit (where the edge street meets the rest of the city). A one-way street pointing away from a junction gets no rules there, since no car arrives that way.

title: How S3 is built and tested
section: How a stop sign finds its street
text:
How a stop sign finds its street



A made-up junction. Left: where a stop sign must stand to belong to a street. Right: how a turn gets its name. To try it on real junctions, open the Lab.


In Québec a stop sign usually stands on the right of the street, just before the junction. S3 relies on that. A post fits an approach when it stands on that same segment, up to 35 m before the junction and 1 to 20 m to the right of the centre line. A post further back belongs to the previous junction. This matters on short pieces, like the 20 m stretches where Wellington splits in two. When several approaches fit, the one closest to the usual spot wins (about 7 m to the right, near the junction), and S3 marks the link as less sure. On a one-way street, signs often stand on both sides, so a post on the left is accepted too. A sign that fits nothing goes on the list to check.

title: How S3 is built and tested
section: How a turn sign finds its street
text:
How a turn sign finds its street
Turn signs often stand across the junction or on a median, so their position is a weak clue. S3 adds a second clue: what the sign would mean on each nearby street. At J027, “left turn only” on Rue Chatham keeps the left onto William and removes the right. On Rue William a car can only go straight on, since Chatham is one-way towards William. There the same sign would remove the only move and trap every car. So the signs belong to Chatham.
A turn sign belongs to a street only when it keeps at least one of its moves and removes at least one. When several streets pass this test, the post decides first. Panels on one post usually face the same drivers. So if a turn sign means something on the street of a stop sign on the same post, it goes to that street. Position decides next. A sign before the junction and on the right is preferred. A sign past the junction is used only when nothing before it fits.
Two panels on one post that contradict each other, like “straight only” above “left or right only”, stand back to back. So the second one looks for another street. If none fits, it goes on the list, since only a photo can tell which way each faces. A turn sign at an exit is ignored, because the streets it points to lie outside the network. If the turn signs on one street together leave no move at all, S3 sets them aside and keeps every move open. After the photo checks, no street is in that state.
My first version placed turn signs by position alone, like stop signs, and left many streets with no way out (X5 repeats it).
To name a turn, S3 compares the arriving heading with the direction of the street the car leaves along. Less than 30° either way counts as straight on. Anything sharper is a left or a right (Chatham onto William turns 89° to the left). S3 never makes a U-turn.

title: How S3 is built and tested
text:
Decisions from photos
For the few signs I could not place from the desk, I wrote down what Mapillary’s street-level photos show (S3 checks with photos). S3 reads those decisions before its own matching, so a photo outranks a guess. The city’s file is never edited. Removing a decision brings back S3’s own matching.

title: How S3 is built and tested
text:
No-entry signs
S1 already takes its one-way streets from the city, so S3 uses no-entry signs only to check S1. A sign agrees when a street near it is one-way towards the junction, or closed to cars. When only a path I added in S1 explains a sign, it goes on the list, because my own decision cannot confirm itself.

title: How S3 is built and tested
text:
Traffic lights
The city’s light file gives each light a point and the names of the streets it stands between. S3 gives each light to the closest junction within 25 m. A light 25 to 100 m from every junction goes on the list, since it may mark a junction S1 is missing. The names give a second check: “Montagne / Wellington” should stand where Rue de la Montagne meets Rue Wellington.

title: How S3 is built and tested
text:
Speed limits
The city’s speed file uses the same street ids as S1, so most segments simply take their own limit. Seven segments have a limit of 0. All seven are closed to cars, so S3 reads 0 as “no limit given”. Three Wellington pieces were redrawn after the file was made and have new ids. For those, S3 takes the speed of lines with the same name lying along the segment within 5 m, when they cover nearly all of it and agree. I chose 5 m by looking at those three segments. It is the smallest distance that covers the two short pieces where Wellington splits. A stress test shows what other distances give.

A disagreement in T6 goes on the list of places to check, because I cannot tell from the desk which source is right. The photos explained the last four.






TipTesting the tests



A test that always passes proves nothing. Before trusting T9 and T10, I broke the data on purpose. I moved one light by 30 m and changed two speed cells: one from 30 to 50, and one empty cell to 0. T9 caught the light and T10 caught both speeds. Then I put the files back.




Stress tests
Each stress test changes one thing on purpose and counts how many rules move. Run twice on the same input (X1), S3 gives identical results.
X2 moves every sign post at random, by up to 1, 2, 4 and 8 m. Up to 2 m, almost nothing changes. At 4 m, ten streets change their stop, and at 8 m, 28 do. So the city’s sign positions would have to be off by more than 2 m to shift the stop rules. I do not know yet how accurate they are, and a few corners are worth checking on the ground.



X2: the further every post moves, the more rules change.


X3 and X4 change how far before the junction, and how far to the right, a sign may stand. Both sit on a plateau, a range where small changes do nothing: a little more or less than my 35 m and 20 m changes no rule. Only the tightest values lose signs. Most signs without a street stand at exits or beyond the edge.
X5 places turn signs by position alone, as my first version did. It leaves 25 streets with no turn at all. With the meaning test and the photo decisions, no street is left that way.
X6 changes how close a light must be to its junction. From 25 to 40 m, the same 31 junctions get lights. At 5 m, eight are lost, mostly on Robert-Bourassa and on edge streets. There the city places the light 5 to 10 m away on a wide corner. At 80 m, lights start landing on the wrong junctions.
X7 changes how far a same-name line may lie when a street is missing from the speed file. It is the one setting with no plateau below it. Under 5 m, two Wellington pieces open to cars lose their limit. From 5 m on, all three redrawn pieces are covered, which is why I chose 5 m (speed limits). Autoroute 10 and its ramps are never in the file, at any distance.

title: S3 Rules
text:
What S3 does
S3 gives the S1 streets their traffic rules. Picture a driver arriving at a junction. S3 answers four questions for them: must I stop here, are there traffic lights, where may I go next, and how fast may I drive. It reads three of the city’s files, and every rule points back to the sign or city record it came from.
The city lists lights and speed limits directly. Stops and turns are harder. The sign file says where each sign stands and what it says. It never says which street the sign faces, and a corner sign often stands close to two or three streets at once. S3 works out the street from where the sign stands and what it would mean there (how S3 is built). Street photos settle the few places I could not decide from the desk (S3 checks with photos).

title: S3 Rules
text:
One junction, step by step
Junction J027 is where Rue Chatham ends at Rue William, in the west of Griffintown.



Rue Chatham is one-way towards William and must stop. Its two turn signs allow only the left.



Three street ends touch J027: Rue Chatham, and Rue William on each side of it. A car can arrive along each, so S3 makes three approaches. An approach is one street, driven towards the corner.
A stop sign stands 10 m before the junction and 5 m to the right of Chatham. That is where a stop sign for Chatham would stand, and it fits no other street. So Chatham must stop.
Two more posts carry “left turn only” signs, both on the right of Chatham, 4 to 8 m before the junction.
From Chatham a car can turn left or right onto William. S3 names each move by how much the car’s heading changes: about 90° to the left is a left.
The signs allow only the left. So the right is forbidden, and the reason is written beside it.
One end of William has its own stop sign and the other has none. So at J027 some streets stop, and there are no lights.

In the Lab, click any junction, then a street arriving at it. You will see each rule with the sign behind it.

Linking a sign to a street is always an inference, so S3 records how sure it is. Most stop signs fit only one street. Turn signs more often went to a best fit, or found no street at all. Lights and stop signs never share a junction. They come from separate files, so that agreement speaks well of both.

title: S3 Rules
text:
What changed in October
S1 gained its edge this month. I also rewrote how a sign finds its street. I suspected my own matching caused the turn conflicts and the no-entry disagreements. The new rules are mostly common sense about how signs are put up. A sign belongs only to a street it actually stands on. Panels on one post face the same drivers unless they contradict each other. Turn signs that fit only one street more than doubled, and the places to check fell from 83 to 27.
Mapillary’s street photos then settled the last turn contradiction, at Wellington and Ann (J006). They also settled every no-entry disagreement, which brought the places to check down to 21.

text:
Places still to check
Seven of the 21 are Autoroute 10 and its ramps, which the city’s speed file does not cover. Six are signs I could not give to any street. Three are signs the photos could not settle (decisions P03 and P06, still open). Three are lights just beyond the edge, such as the one at Queen and Wellington. Two are recent no-entry posts at the park connectors, newer than every photo. Signs at exits that face streets beyond the network are left off, since they are not mine to check.

title: S3 Rules
text:
What S3 does not know
The city’s file says where the lights are and nothing about their timing. Movement counts and light timing estimates the timing where the city counted traffic. Elsewhere, the cycle will be a procedural assumption in S9: a rule I set for the simulation. Some turn rules hold only at certain hours. S3 keeps them on at all hours until S9 runs its imagined drivers by the clock of S5 Rhythm.
An exit is where an edge street meets the rest of the city, and S3 cannot see the streets beyond it. A junction there may look like an all-way stop when a street beyond does not stop. The junction’s note says so.

title: S4 Buildings
text:
Asks What each building is used for, how tall it is, how many people live in it, and where a walker reaches it.

Stands verified: 9 tests pass. The dwellings come within about 1 % of a provincial land-use file, checked in aggregate.
Leaves out 61 cases still to check by hand, most of them buildings no source describes.
In the game World: building masses with a height and a door (G1 World, verified). Points: places to go (planned).

title: S4 Buildings
text:
What S4 does
S4 says what each building in the study area is: what it is used for, how tall it is, how many people live in it, and what is on its ground floor. S1 to S3 say where people can move. They say nothing about why anyone would go somewhere. A street is busy at noon because of what lines it: a bank, a café, a gym, five hundred condos. S5 Rhythm reads S4 to know which places open when. S7 will read it for where trips start and end.
Most answers come from the city’s tax roll, the official list of every property and what it is. When the roll is silent, I fall back on OpenStreetMap, the open map anyone can edit. The ground floor comes from the city’s 2025 survey of street-level commercial spaces. Each answer keeps its source. A value no file knows stays empty, with the reason. One value is an assumption: no open file says where the doors are, so I link each building to the nearest walkable street. How S4 is built gives every source and rule.

title: S4 Buildings
text:
One building, step by step
District Griffin sur Peel is the long low block on Rue Peel between Ottawa and William, with towers on top. OpenStreetMap draws it as one outline tagged retail. The tax roll places 496 properties on its lot. Of these, 494 are condo dwellings. The other two are a shopping centre and a condo parking space. The roll speaks first, so S4 calls the building residential. It keeps the retail tag on record, unused.
The 2025 survey finds ten premises on the ground floor, among them three banks and two restaurants. One space is vacant. Seven of the shops also appear in OpenStreetMap under the same name, and S4 counts each once. The nearest walkable street is Rue Ottawa, 6.5 m away.
This block shows the main weakness of S4. Counted by property, the condos outvote the shops 494 to 1. Yet on the street, the block reads as a shopping strip. So S4 keeps the ground floor apart from the use. “Used for” says what most of the building is. “Ground floor” says what a walker passes.

title: S4 Buildings
text:
What it found
There are 296 buildings in the study area. The tax roll gave the use of 188, and OpenStreetMap of 74. The other 34 stay unknown, mostly small sheds and annexes. Most buildings with a known use are residential. Together they hold 11,954 dwellings. The stress tests show this total is steadier than any single tower’s count.
In the Lab, the S4 tab colours the buildings by use or by source. Click one to see each value with its source. You also see the places inside it and its street.

UseSource





What each building is used for. Pink dashed outline: no source says. Pink X: B01, 415 properties at one address with no outline.







Where each building’s use came from. White means the tax roll and grey means OpenStreetMap. Pink dashed means no source, so the use stays unknown.

title: S4 Buildings
section: What I still need to check
text:
What I still need to check
S4 flags 61 cases for me to look at by hand. They are also listed in the Lab. Most are buildings whose use no source gives. Some are ties between two uses. A few stand far from any walkable street, Hangar 1825 most of all. In ten, the lot and the address point name different buildings. The largest of these, Griffix, is why S4 now reads the lot first.
The case that matters most is 1485 rue des Bassins (B01). It has 415 properties built in 2024, 290 dwellings and 125 condo parking spaces, all at one address point with no building on it. I first took it for a building OpenStreetMap had not drawn yet. The lot outlines changed my reading. The lot of 1485 holds Bass 4 and Le Vittorio, 130 m from the address point. Neither tower has a single property placed in it. So the dwellings most likely belong to those two towers, and the address point is what is out of place (partial). No file says which tower holds how many. Until a door number or a site visit settles it, I leave them unplaced and outside the 11,954 dwellings. I split nothing by guess.

Stands verified: 12 tests pass. The counts’ bicycle shape follows the detectors’ (correlation 0.89).
Leaves out Weekends and seasons on foot and by car. Lingering escapes every count.
In the game Rhythm: opening hours time the NPCs. Check: the counts stay out of the game and test it (planned).

title: S5 Rhythm
text:
What S5 does
S5 gives each hour of the week what the open data says about it. Henri Lefebvre proposed reading a city through its rhythms, the repetitions of days and seasons (Lefebvre 2004). S5 is the first Situ system that holds time, and it keeps two kinds of evidence apart.
The first is measured: how busy the streets are, hour by hour, from the city’s movement counts at S1 junctions, the points where streets meet. The second is promised: the opening hours S4 gathered. A count records one day. An opening hour records an intention, and a place can be open and empty. S5 never mixes the two, so a later system always knows which one it is reading.
Neither is a simulation. The promised hours can time the walkers and drivers S9 will imagine. The measured day stays out of them, so S9 can compare what they do with it.

title: S5 Rhythm
text:
What was measured

9 counted days at 7 junctions · no weekend


Counts: the days on which the city counted people and vehicles at S1 junctions, between 8 February 2024 and 12 May 2026, in its intersection counts file.
Does not show: an ordinary week. Six of the seven junctions were counted on a single day.

The city counted seven S1 junctions on nine days, all from Tuesday to Thursday. Only J040, where Guy meets Ottawa and William, was counted around the clock, for three days in December 2024. The other six were counted on one day each, in three windows covering both rush hours and midday.
Junctions differ in size: J051 on Notre-Dame sees about four times the people of J006 on Ann. So S5 compares shapes. Each day is divided by its own average over the six hours every day counted (7h, 8h, 11h, 12h, 16h and 17h), which makes 1.0 an ordinary daytime hour of that day. A weekday hour then takes the mean of the days that counted it, with their lowest and highest. How S5 is built gives the rules.



A weekday, hour by hour. White: the mean of the counted days. Grey band: lowest to highest. Pink: hours counted at J040 alone.


Every weekday hour has a value, but 17 of the 24 rest on J040’s three December days alone (verified). From 18:00 to 6:00, the shape is one junction in winter.
My first reading, and it is an interpretation: people on foot have a sharper evening than morning, peaking at 17h at about one and a half times an ordinary hour, against just over one at 8h. Bicycles peak at 8h and 17h, while cars spread their busy hours from 16h to 19h. On Wellington, where four junctions were counted on one Thursday in February, Murray and Young carried the most vehicles at 8h, and Ann and Shannon at 17h. Only one day stands behind that difference, so it stays a question for the field.

title: S5 Rhythm
section: Bicycles, every day of the year
text:
Bicycles, every day of the year

376 days from 3 detectors · 59 Saturdays and 57 Sundays


Counts: the days on which all three bicycle detectors in the area recorded every hour, between 9 June 2025 and 14 October 2026, from the city’s permanent bicycle counters.
Does not show: walking or driving. Two of the detectors stand at one place, Peel at Ottawa, one per direction.

The city also keeps permanent bicycle detectors that record every hour of every day. Three stand inside the study area: two on Peel at Ottawa, one per direction, and one on William at Nazareth, westbound. All three were complete on 376 days between 9 June 2025 and 14 October 2026, so for bicycles S5 can speak about weekends and seasons. Each day is read like the counts, against its own reference hours.



Bicycles all year. Above: the shape of the day, by kind of day and season. Below: bicycles on an average day, month by month.


The year swings hard (verified, for these three detectors). An average day in August or September brings about 1,800 to 1,900 bicycles past them. From December to February it brings 130 to 180, roughly ten times fewer. The week matters less: in summer a Saturday brings nine tenths of a weekday’s bicycles, and a Sunday about three quarters.
The kind of day changes the shape more than the amount. Weekdays, in every season, peak sharply at 8h and 17h. Saturdays and Sundays have no morning peak: bicycles build to a long afternoon, highest from 13h to 17h. My reading, and it is an interpretation: on weekdays these streets carry a commute, and on weekends an outing.
The two sources agree where they meet. On weekdays the counts’ bicycle shape follows the detectors’ closely, with a correlation of 0.89 over the 24 hours, where 1 would mean the two move in perfect step (partial: the agreement is probably real, since the streets and the years differ). The largest gap is at 19h in winter, where the counts rest on J040 alone. Two more detectors stand on Peel at Notre-Dame, just outside the area, and S5 leaves them out.

title: S5 Rhythm
text:
What the places promise

83 of 558 places give their hours


Counts: the places S4 found that publish opening hours: 79 through OpenStreetMap and 4 through the city’s list of public places.
Does not show: whether a place keeps its hours. The other 475 stay unknown at every hour.

Of the 558 places S4 found, 83 give opening hours (15 %), almost all through OpenStreetMap. Restaurants and cafés lead, then mostly shops, bars, banks and parks. The other 475 stay unknown at every hour: S5 never reads a missing hour as closed.



Places open each hour of the week, among the 83 that give hours. A place counts as open in an hour when it is open at half past.


The promised week peaks around midday from Tuesday to Friday, with 73 places open, and thins to about 56 on Sunday. By 21h fewer than 30 remain. Two places give hours S5 cannot read with certainty, so they become checkpoints, cases set aside for a closer look. Henden opens at 19:00 with no closing time (H01). SHAY’s brunch rule, read the way the tag’s grammar says, replaces its weekend dinner hours (H02).

title: S5 Rhythm
text:
The ring around the area
Between November 2024 and May 2026 the city counted 23 more intersections outside the study area, within 600 m of its edge (verified). S5 keeps them as a ring, read exactly like the counts inside. They build nothing: they let S9 compare what it imagines with what was counted just beyond the area.



The ring: weekday pedestrians at 8 h at the intersections counted around the area (squares) and at the S1 junctions inside it (circles).


The ring is lopsided. Towards Old Montréal, along McGill and at Square-Victoria, the counts reach 1,000 to 2,355 pedestrians at 8 h, more than at any junction inside the area. Across the canal, on Saint-Patrick and in Pointe-Saint-Charles, they stay under 110. Most ring sites were counted on one or two weekdays in September, November, December or May, and the junctions inside mostly in February and December. So the two sides of the edge also differ by season.
Fifteen of the ring’s counted days are Saturdays. S5 keeps them apart from the weekdays: they are the only Saturday counts of people on foot near the area.

title: S5 Rhythm
text:
What S5 cannot say yet
The bicycles now have weekends and seasons. People on foot and cars have Saturdays only in the ring. The places say Saturday is almost as open as a weekday, and no count of walkers tells whether people come. The counts fall in February, May, November and December, while the bicycles show how much summer changes a street. The three detectors stand on Peel and William, and cycling on the canal path may keep another rhythm. Lingering escapes every count, since a count records people passing a point and says nothing of those who stay.
The rhythm diaries and rhythm maps of my fieldwork will add a third kind of evidence, people’s own account of their week, once ethics approval comes (Limits of the desk).

title: S5 Rhythm
text:
In the Lab
In the Lab, the S5 tab sets a day and an hour. Places light up when they say they are open, and each counted junction grows with that hour’s count. Play the day to watch it fill and empty. On a Saturday or Sunday the junctions inside stay empty rings, since nothing was counted there, while the ring’s squares show their Saturday counts. Switch to bicycles and pick a season, and the three detectors grow with the hour on any day of the week.

text:

Found 971 trees, 104 hydrants, 806 street lights and 487 sidewalk pieces. Most trees with a date were planted in 2013 or later.
Stands verified: 7 tests pass. Photo detections found 68 of the city’s 104 hydrants.
Leaves out Trees on private land, and what no photo shows.
In the game World: 2,783 props and the sidewalks (G1 World, verified). Points: seats and tables (planned).

title: S6 Streetscape
text:
What S6 does
S6 records what stands on Griffintown’s streets besides the buildings: trees, fire hydrants, benches and other furniture, street lights, surveillance cameras, pedestrian crossings, the sidewalks and traffic islands themselves, and the road works under way on the day I saved the city’s list. Each object keeps its source and the values that source gives, and is linked to the S1 street it stands on.
S6 decides nothing about what these objects do. A tree may shade a walker or hide a shop; a hydrant means no car may stop beside it. Those effects are assumptions, so they belong to S9, which will write each one down. What a walker can see from where they stand comes from the system after S7, built from the S4 buildings and these trees.

title: S6 Streetscape
text:
What it found

971 trees · 104 hydrants · 806 street lights · 487 sidewalk pieces · 29 road works


Counts: objects inside the study area. Trees, hydrants, sidewalks and road works come from the city’s files saved on 16 October 2026. Street lights come from OpenStreetMap and from Mapillary’s photo detections, each light counted once.
Does not show: everything that stands there. Trees on private land are missing, and the detections miss what no photo shows.




What stands on the streets. White circles: older or undated trees. Grey: trees planted since 2013, each sized by its trunk. Pink: hydrants and road works.


The streetscape is young (verified, for what the city records). Of the 775 public trees with a planting date, 651 were planted in 2013 or later, and three quarters of all trunks are less than 18 cm across. Of the 267 sidewalk pieces with a construction date, 175 were built in 2020 or later. The commonest species are elms, honey-locusts, poplars and Kentucky coffeetrees.
My reading, and it is an interpretation: Griffintown’s street furniture is as new as its towers, and its trees are still small. A view along a street today is probably more open than it will be in twenty years. Any study of what can be seen here describes one moment in a growing place.
All 286 pieces of furniture, from benches and bicycle racks to drinking fountains, come from OpenStreetMap, since the city’s furniture file covers only its large parks. Mappers may have missed some (assumption). On 16 October 2026 the city listed 29 road works in the area, from sidewalk rebuilding on Saint-Martin to construction on Young that runs until June 2027.

title: S6 Streetscape
text:
Read by a machine

Street lights
The city publishes no file of its street lights (verified, for its open data catalogue). OpenStreetMap records 72 in the area. Mapillary is a site where people and the city upload street photos. Its software scans every photo for objects, street lights among them, and places each one on the map. It found street lights in 888 places here. Detections less than 3 m apart are joined into one light, since a pole often carries two heads, which leaves 764. Counting each light found by either source once, the area has 806.



Street lights. White: found in photos by Mapillary’s software. Grey: the same, found in no photo since 2023. Pink rings: lamps in OpenStreetMap.


The hydrants show how far the machine can be trusted, since the city’s file lists every one. Mapillary’s software found 82 hydrants, and 68 of them stand within 5 m of one of the city’s, half of them less than a metre away. So it found 68 of the city’s 104. Where its photos reach, it is mostly right and well placed, and it misses about a third (partial; some misses may be streets no photo covers).
The two sources of lights barely meet. Only 30 of OpenStreetMap’s 72 lamps have a detection within 5 m. Most of the others line the east end of Rue des Bassins and Allée des Barges, where the sheet shows almost no detections. Those are walking streets beside the basins, and most photos are taken from cars (assumption). The machine sees what the camera passed, so a walker’s street may be the one it knows least.


Crossings and cameras
The same software finds surveillance cameras and the paint of pedestrian crossings, and OpenStreetMap records both. The two agree on crossings, and barely on cameras.



Cameras and crossings. Filled marks: found in photos by Mapillary’s software, fainter when no photo since 2023 shows them. Rings: the same kinds in OpenStreetMap.


Crossings are where the machine and the mappers meet. Of the 102 painted crossings Mapillary’s software found, 74 stand within 5 m of a crossing OpenStreetMap records as painted or signalled, half of them less than 2 m away. OpenStreetMap records 481 crossings, 289 of them unmarked, and the photos find 83 of its 192 painted ones. Six painted crossings in the photos stand where OpenStreetMap says there is no paint: either a crossing painted since, or a tag nobody updated (assumption).
The cameras barely overlap. The photos show 34 and OpenStreetMap has 55, with only 2 in both. Most of OpenStreetMap’s cameras are tagged as private outdoor cameras along Wellington, Young and Murray, probably mapped by someone reading building fronts (assumption). A few are the city’s traffic cameras at corners of Peel and de la Montagne. The software’s cameras spread across the area, six of them on Rue William. Each source finds a different set of watchers, and neither finds them all.
The software also finds poles, and S6 leaves them out. The street lights already show which streets are lit, and the number of poles depends mostly on how close two detections must be to count as one.


Street furniture
For benches and bicycle racks, the machine and the mappers agree too little for either to fill the other’s gaps. Bins are the same: Mapillary’s software finds 320 where OpenStreetMap has 38, and many are probably household bins set out on collection day (assumption). S6 keeps those detections out of its objects and reports the comparison in its tests.

title: S6 Streetscape
text:
What S6 leaves out
The city’s tree inventory covers public trees only, so trees in courtyards and on private land are missing. The city’s canopy model and its aerial LiDAR, a laser scan from the air, date from 2015, before most of today’s towers and trees, so S6 does not use them. The city’s art data holds a single subsidized mural in the area and none of its own public art collection. The artworks OpenStreetMap records are already among the S4 places. The city publishes no file of its street lights, so S6 takes them from OpenStreetMap and from photos.

title: S6 Streetscape
text:
Checkpoints
Checkpoints are cases set aside for a closer look. Five road works are still listed although their permits ended the day before I saved the file (K01 to K05). They may have been extended, or the list may lag behind the street. Thirty-five objects were found only in photos taken before 2023 (K06 to K40): 26 street lights, 6 painted crossings and 3 cameras. Griffintown has been rebuilt street by street since then, and some may be gone.

title: S6 Streetscape
text:
In the Lab
In the Lab, the S6 tab draws the sidewalks under the streets, coloured by material or by the year they were built. Every tree, hydrant, piece of furniture, light, camera, crossing and road work sits on top, as a coloured dot from afar and as its own small icon once you zoom in. Click anything to see its source and values. How S6 is built gives the rules and the tests.

title: S7 Commuters
text:
Asks Who commutes from and to Griffintown on a weekday, how, when, and how far each home is from transit.
Found About 7,200 residents commute, a quarter on foot. 71 % of homes are more than 800 m from a metro entrance.
Stands verified: 6 tests pass. Not yet compared with commuting observed on the street.
Leaves out Where anyone goes. The census week of May 2021 fell during the pandemic.
In the game Rhythm: how many NPCs leave home, by which mode and when (planned).

title: S7 Commuters
text:
What S7 does
From the open data, S7 says who commutes from Griffintown and to it on an ordinary weekday. For each building, it gives how many residents go out to work and how they travel. It also gives the hour they leave and each home’s walk to the metro and the bus along the S1 streets. For people who work here, it gives how they come and when they arrive.
S7 draws no walks. No open file says where each person goes and by which street, or when they come back. Imagining that belongs to S9, which will tell the neighbourhood’s story from all the systems. S7 also reads neither the city’s counts nor space syntax, the measures of how each street sits in the whole network, so that S9 can compare with them. What a walker can see from the street belongs to S8.

title: S7 Commuters
text:
What it found

about 7,200 residents commute, a quarter on foot · 71 % of homes are more than 800 m from a metro entrance


Counts: an estimate of the residents who leave the area’s homes for work on a weekday, and the share of homes more than 800 m from a metro entrance along S1’s streets. It comes from the 2021 census for four tracts, scaled to S4’s 11,954 homes with a correction for working from home, and from the STM schedule of October 2026.
Does not show: where anyone goes. The shares by mode come from May 2021 and may give the car too much today (assumption).




Every building with homes, sized by its residents who commute on a weekday today. The white dot inside shows those who walk all the way to work. Grey squares are bus stops.


The 11,954 homes in S4 send about 7,200 residents out to work on a weekday. About a quarter walk all the way and close to half drive, while a fifth take the metro or a bus (partial, for the reasons under What it rests on). Most leave between 7 and 9 in the morning.
No metro entrance stands inside the area. Half of the homes are more than 940 m from the nearest one along the streets, and 71 % are more than 800 m away. Yet no home is more than about 400 m from a bus stop (verified, for the streets of S1). Bonaventure is the nearest metro for half of the homes and Lucien-L’Allier for a third. Georges-Vanier is nearest for the rest.



When commuters leave and arrive, in the census’s own hour bands. Above: residents leaving for work. Below: people arriving to work here. Both by mode.


About 5,000 people work in the three census tracts (the small areas the census reports on) that cover most of the area. Close to 60 % of them come by car. A fifth come by metro, and fewer than one in ten on foot. They arrive a little later than the residents leave, most of them between 7:30 and 10.
My reading, and it is an interpretation: Griffintown’s residents walk to work far more than the people who work here, and its homes are close to buses and far from the metro. The neighbourhood seems to send walkers out and take drivers in.

title: S7 Commuters
text:
What it rests on
The census of May 2021 is the only open source that says, tract by tract, how people travel to work and at what hour they leave or arrive (verified). Its week fell during the pandemic, and 42 to 56 % of the employed residents of the three tracts worked from home. Across Canada, working from home fell from 24 % in that week to 17 % in May 2025. S7 applies that fall to each tract once, so a tract where 55 % worked from home now counts about 39 %. That is its one correction, and every number of commuters moves with it; the stress test shows by how much. The shares by mode and by hour stay the census’s own.
In 2021 people probably avoided transit, so the shares by mode probably give the car too much today (assumption). The 2026 census should replace all of this, but its commuting results will likely come out after this prototype ends.
The number of homes is today’s, from the tax roll in S4, so the towers built since 2021 are counted.

title: S7 Commuters
text:
Checkpoints
None. Every building with homes lies in a tract where people lived at the 2021 census.

title: S7 Commuters
text:
In the Lab
In the Lab, the S7 tab draws every building with homes, sized by its commuters: all of them, or one way of travelling at a time. Click a building to see its commuters by mode and its walk to the nearest metro entrance and bus stop. The side panel lists the census’s hour bands.

title: S8 Views
text:
Asks What a person on a walkable street can see, measured on the open map.
Found The views split the area in two: 5,000 to 13,000 m² in the old grid, 90,000 to 115,000 m² along the canal. Almost every view is a corridor.
Stands verified: 6 tests pass. Not compared with what walkers notice.
Leaves out Trees, fences, parked trucks and rail structures stop no sight line. A building missing from the map opens a view that is not there.
In the game Points: where a view opens along a route, a candidate pause (planned).
Trace How it is built · run record · uses S1 · feeds S9

title: S8 Views
text:
What S8 does
S8 asks what a person on a walkable street can see, using the open map. Every 10 m along each walkable S1 street in the area, it casts 360 sight lines. Each runs until it meets a building outline or reaches 300 m. The shape they enclose is an isovist: the part of the city visible from one spot (Benedikt 1979). S8 gives each viewpoint its area, its longest and mean sight line, and how compact the shape is. Each street gets the mean of its viewpoints.
S8 only measures. Who looks, and what an open or closed view does to a walk, belong to S9. Like S7, S8 reads neither the city’s counts nor space syntax, so S9 can compare it with both.

title: S8 Views
text:
What it found

1,798 viewpoints · median area seen 32,000 m², the middle 80 % between 9,500 and 109,000 m²


Counts: viewpoints every 10 m along the walkable S1 streets, and the area each one sees within 300 m along 360 sight lines. The walls come from OpenStreetMap’s building outlines, saved on 14 October 2026.
Does not show: what a walker notices. Trees, fences, parked trucks and the rail structures stop no sight line here, and a building missing from the map opens a view that is not there.




Walkable streets in the area, coloured by mean area seen: dark is most enclosed, light pink most open. Grey streets are not walkable or lie outside the area.


The views split the neighbourhood in two (verified, for the map S8 reads). The small streets of the old grid (Eleanor, du Shannon, Barré, Murray and Young) see 5,000 to 13,000 m² from a typical viewpoint. The canal edge sees 90,000 to 115,000 m², and so do Rue Smith and Boulevard Robert-Bourassa. Rue Wellington and Rue Ann sit in between at about 50,000 m², with Rue des Bassins.
Almost every view is a corridor. From 95 % of viewpoints, at least one sight line runs the full 300 m along the street. The median compactness is 0.10, where a circle scores 1. The canal path is the most rounded, at about 0.2, because the water opens the view sideways.



The most enclosed view (Rue Payette) and the most open (Rue de la Commune Ouest), with the median (Rue des Bassins).


A street’s mean hides how its view changes as you walk. On 49 of the 231 segments, the most open viewpoint sees over three times as much as the most enclosed. This is usually where the street crosses another or passes an empty lot.
My reading, and it is an interpretation: the old grid keeps the long, narrow views of a nineteenth-century working district, and the redevelopment along the canal opened wide views towards the water and the expressways. Whether people walk differently through the two is a question for S9 and the counts.

title: S8 Views
text:
What it rests on
Only OpenStreetMap’s building outlines stop a sight line. Trees, fences, parked trucks and the rail and expressway structures at the south-east corner are not in that file. They stop nothing, so views there are wider than a person would see (partial). I left trees out on purpose: the city records their trunks, and nothing open says how wide their crowns are today. The view is flat, at eye level: a low wall blocks a sight line just as a tower does.
A building missing from OpenStreetMap opens a view that does not exist. The stress test left out one outline in ten at random. The median area seen grew by 13 to 78 %, and in each draw one street saw three to nearly eight times as much. The order of the streets held better (rank correlation 0.90 to 0.99, where 1 means the same order). So I trust how streets rank more than any single area (partial).
The 300 m reach is my choice. At 100 m or 500 m the areas change a lot, but the order of the streets stays close (0.95 and 0.99).

title: S9 Observer
text:
What S9 does
S9 is the mother-analyzer. The systems before it hold the open data I could find from my desk, with as few assumptions as I could manage. S9 is where I imagine: it combines them into flows of people, and only then compares those flows with what the city counted and with space syntax.
Imagining needs rules. S9 writes each one in a ledger with its source, or marks it as an assumption. It builds rival readings, each changing one rule, so a difference between them points at that rule. No reading is tuned to the counts or space syntax: a test scrambles both and nothing moves.
S9 grows in slices. The first is a weekday morning on foot.

title: S9 Observer
text:
What it found

commuters make up about a quarter of the pedestrians counted at 7 and 8 h · the busiest counted junction gets none of them


Counts: S9’s imagined commuters at the seven junctions the city counted, as a share of the pedestrians counted there at 7 and 8 h. The commuters come from S7, routed on S1 under three rival rules.
Does not show: that the routes are right. They rest on the assumptions in the ledger, and six of the seven junctions were counted on one day.




The morning’s commuters on each street in the reading “shortest”. Pink circles are the junctions the city counted, sized by pedestrians at 8 h.


At the seven counted junctions, S9’s commuters make up 22 to 27 % of the pedestrians counted, whichever reading routes them (verified, for these rules). The rest are people this slice does not hold: errands, school runs, dog walks, visitors and people crossing from beyond the area. The counts give the size of that gap, and later slices will try to fill it.
The busiest counted junction, Robert-Bourassa at Saint-Jacques, saw 868 pedestrians at 8 h. No S9 commuter passes there, in any reading or stress test. It lies just north of the area, beyond the doors S9’s walkers take towards downtown and the metro. Its walkers come from outside this slice, probably from Old Montréal or from beyond the area to the east (assumption). It is the clearest question this slice raises, and it is listed as a checkpoint.
Where commuters do pass, they explain more: half to three quarters of the count at Guy and Ottawa (the one junction counted on three days), and a third to a half at de la Montagne and Notre-Dame, on the road to Lucien-L’Allier and Bonaventure.



What the commuters explain at each counted junction at 8 h, in each reading.


The four Wellington junctions were counted on the same February morning. Their counts are even, from 221 to 303 pedestrians at 8 h. The shortest routes crowd the commuters onto Rue Young (164) and leave Rue du Shannon almost empty (18), a ninefold spread. The fewest-turns routes spread them out to a threefold one. Four junctions on one day settle nothing, so I read this as a lead: walkers here may use the parallel streets more evenly than the shortest walk predicts (assumption, a lead).



Where the readings move walkers off the shortest routes: pink where more walk, grey where fewer.


“Open” changes the route of 13 % of walkers, mostly from Rue Young to the more open Rue Peel, and adds three metres to the median walk. “Straight” changes 34 % and sends some on long detours: 15 % walk more than a quarter further than needed. In a grid this tight, the view matters little to a commuter’s route, and counting turns alone sends walkers further than people would plausibly accept.
Walking choice, in space syntax, is how often a street lies on the way between other places. The morning’s flows agree with it only weakly: rank correlation 0.24 for the shortest routes and 0.29 for the fewest turns, where 1 means the same order (verified, as computed). Choice counts every route between every pair of streets. The morning sends everyone to a few doors and stations, so flows bunch on Peel and de la Montagne where choice is spread out.
My reading, and it is an interpretation: in the morning, Griffintown’s streets carry commuters mostly as a way out, towards the stations and downtown. Most of the pedestrians counted are doing something else.

title: What space syntax is
text:
Space syntax began with Bill Hillier and Julienne Hanson at University College London. Their book The Social Logic of Space (1984) argued that the way spaces are arranged carries social meaning, and that it can be measured. In a city, the method asks two questions about every street: how easy it is to reach from everywhere else, and how often it lies on the way between other places.
It looks at the shape of the network and nothing else. I find that limit useful. It lets me ask how much of Griffintown’s movement the layout alone can explain.

title: What space syntax is
text:
Space syntax began with Bill Hillier and Julienne Hanson at University College London. Their book The Social Logic of Space (1984) argued that the way spaces are arranged carries social meaning, and that it can be measured. In a city, the method asks two questions about every street: how easy it is to reach from everywhere else, and how often it lies on the way between other places.
It looks at the shape of the network and nothing else. I find that limit useful. It lets me ask how much of Griffintown’s movement the layout alone can explain.

title: What space syntax is
text:
Segments and depth
The unit is the segment: a piece of street between two junctions, as in S1 Streets. Depth is the distance between two segments, counted by how much you turn. A right angle costs 1 and a 45° turn costs 0.5 (Turner 2007, p. 542). Hillier and Iida (2005) found that counting turns matched observed movement better than counting metres. Turner also showed that ordinary street centrelines can be analysed this way, so I can use the city’s own street file.

title: What space syntax is
text:
Integration and choice
Integration measures how close a segment is, on average, to every other segment. A street with high integration is easy to get to. Network science calls this closeness centrality (Sabidussi 1966).
Choice imagines the shortest route between every pair of segments and counts how many of those routes pass through each one. A street with high choice is often passed through. Network science calls this betweenness centrality (Freeman 1977).
The results also include normalised versions (Hillier, Yang & Turner 2012, pp. 160, 165 and 191). NAIN rescales integration so that networks of different sizes can be compared. NACH does the same for choice. It also evens out a skew in choice, where a few streets score very high and most score low. The paper gives two versions of NAIN, so I compare NAIN numbers only within one version (Reading closely).

title: What space syntax is
text:
Natural movement
Hillier, Penn, Hanson, Grajewski and Xu (1993) called their central claim “natural movement”. It says the shape of the network is a main driver of how many people walk each street. The full references are in Resources.






NoteStill debated



The claim is influential, and its strength varies with place and land use. In the 1993 paper itself, the correlation between integration and movement across ten parts of King’s Cross ranged from 0.25 to 0.80. Shops could also multiply movement beyond what the layout predicts (Hillier et al. 1993, pp. 31, 46). Ratti (2004, p. 492) adds that results depend on how the map is drawn, and that the method leaves land use out. So in Situ the claim is something I test in Griffintown.

title: What space syntax is
text:
Radius
The analysis can be limited to a distance around each segment, called the radius. At 400 m it asks how central a street is within about five minutes’ walk. Radius n has no limit, which here means the whole island. Studies usually take 400 to 800 m as the low radius and 4,000 to 8,000 m as the high one (van Nes & Yamu 2021, p. 65). For walking I use 200, 400 and 800 m and radius n. For driving I use 1200 and 2000 m. A street can be central at 400 m and remote at radius n. That contrast often tells me more than any single value.

title: What space syntax is
text:
A made-up town
I invented this town so the numbers can be checked by hand. Here depth counts one step per change of street. The town has a main street (M1 to M5), cross streets to the north and south, a back street (B1, B2) and a cul-de-sac (C1, C2).



The made-up town, drawn once for each measure in the tabs below.



DepthIntegrationChoice


Start from M1 at depth 0. Every street one step away has depth 1, the next ones depth 2, and so on. C2, at the end of the cul-de-sac, is six steps away.


M3 has the highest integration (0.55), because it sits in the middle. C2 has the lowest (0.24), because every other street is far from it.


M4 has the highest choice (55). Routes from the west side to the east side and to the cul-de-sac must all cross it. C1 has 15, since every route to C2 passes through it. A dead end like C2 scores 0.









TipWhat the toy shows



M3 is the best place to be, and M4 is the best place to pass through. The two measures differ, so I keep both.

title: What space syntax is
text:
Why I use it

A measuring stick
My simulated walkers (agents) never read space syntax values. I compare their movement with the values afterwards, so the comparison is a real test. If the agents preferred high-scoring streets, the test would be circular: the answer would go in and come back out.
Choice is already a route model. It is built on the route with the least turning between every pair of segments (Turner 2007, p. 544). Walkers who took those routes, spread evenly over all pairs, would match choice by construction, and the match would prove nothing. So the walkers S9 imagines pick routes for their own reasons, such as where they are going and the time of day. Space syntax enters Situ only at the end, in S9 Observer.


What the comparison can show

Where the walkers and choice agree, the layout alone may explain the movement. Where they disagree, something else is at work, such as a building or a rule.


The city’s movement counts check the model against reality, and they are thin: seven S1 junctions, one to three days each, between February 2024 and May 2026. They are enough to raise a warning and too few to prove anything.


In the game I can watch whether players drift toward well-integrated streets, the ones that are easy to reach. That bears on my research question about wayfinding.





Why this method
It runs in QGIS on the city’s open street file, and the same file with the same settings gives the same values. Forty years of studies use it, so I can set Griffintown beside other cities. It was built to study how layout and social life relate, which is the subject of my research. Its blind spots are well documented, and each one is handled by another Situ system.


What this means for my data
Values belong to the network they were calculated on. A missing path makes its neighbours look less connected than they are. So I added the city’s off-street paths before the analysis (The walking network).
The edge of the map also distorts. Streets near it look remote only because the map stops there (Ratti 2004, p. 496; van Nes & Yamu 2021, p. 51). So the analysis covers the whole island, and I cut Griffintown out of the results afterwards.
